eat.desc: Extremely good pizza with a nice selection of craft and in-house beers on tap. 10 flagship beers with variety of rotating selections. They have expanded across Montana with canned beer, so you can enjoy these brews wherever you end up. Has balcony seating area (not recommended in the winter) and a bar. Live music sometimes as well.

eat.name: Mountains Walking
eat.desc: Locally made beer. Brewer is "interested in beers made with living cultures that have naturally lower alcohol and sugar levels" leading to an eclectic range of beers on tap.

see.name: Caras Park
see.desc: The park is a hub of city festivities and intimate concerts, with brick plazas, restrooms and a pavilion. It is on land reclaimed when the Higgins Avenue Bridge was widened in 1962. Next to the park is '''A Carousel for Missoula''', a wooden, hand-carved and volunteer-built carousel.

see.name: Historical Museum at Fort Missoula
see.desc: Explore the 32-acre park and museum showcasing Missoula area history. Museum features rotating exhibits. Over 20 preserved historic buildings of the fort and World War II internment camp. Walking tour of the fort always available and free. Come in late April for the annual forestry day to watch professional competitors in timber sports like log rolling and speed climbing. If you've never watched these lumberjack events, they are incredibly fun spectator sports.

see.name: Missoula Art Museum
see.desc: Worth a visit. Knowing that it could never outbid its big-city counterparts for works by famous artists, the museum has instead hosts regularly-rotated exhibits of Western art and works closely with community arts groups. Furthermore, the price is right for visitors, as demonstrated by its slogan: ''Free Expression, Free Admission''.

see.name: Missoula County Courthouse
see.desc: This historic courthouse building has eight original murals by E.S. Paxson.

see.name: Montana Museum of Art & Culture
see.desc: Rotating permanent collection and outside artwork. Website has a campus artwalk map. The collections held in several buildings, check website for current locations.

see.name: Milwaukee Railway Station
see.desc: This former depot built by the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul & Pacific Railroad is used by the Boone & Crockett Club.

see.name: Northern Pacific Railway Station
see.desc: This former depot is used as office space by local businesses and home of the Missoula Farmer's Market during the summer months.

see.name: First Friday
see.desc: Find art galleries open to strolling passersby with music and food offered for free.

see.name: Splash Montana
see.desc: City owned waterpark. Three 3-story waterslides, lazy river, play structures plus Olympic sized pool. Café and grill.

see.name: Missoula Paddleheads
see.desc: Enjoy a Pioneer League baseball game at Orgren Park at Allegiance Field.

see.name: MOBASH Skatepark
see.desc: Lit at night and featuring a cradle, Built by Grindline.

see.name: Blue Mountain Disc Golf
see.desc: 18 holes of disc golf on a very hilly, wooded course. Cross the street to take the '''Maclay Flat Nature Trail'''. For a beginner course try '''Meadow Hill Middle School''' ''(4210 S Reserve St)''.

see.name: Fort Missoula Regional Park
see.desc: City park and sport complex. There are tennis courts, pickleball courts, outdoor fitness center, lawn volleyball, disc golf at this 156-acre park. Plus 3 playgrounds and a dog park.

see.name: Pattee Canyon Recreation Area
see.desc: Extensive trail system covering 27 miles is open to any non-motorized use. Used by cross-country skiers in winter. Nearby disc golf course. Picnic area with vault toilets, but no water, at trailhead.

see.name: Kim Williams Trail
see.desc: This trail is an easy way to appreciate the Clark Fork River.

see.name: Mt. Sentinel
see.desc: Mt. Sentinel offers a scenic trail system. A trail starting at the University of Montana leads 700 feet up the mountainside to the "M," which offers great views of the city. More adventurous hikers may continue another 1400 feet to the peak of Mount Sentinel, which offers great views of the city, the Rattlesnake Wilderness to the north, and Mount Jumbo to the north. Those with binoculars may perceive the ancient shoreline of Lake Missoula on Mount Jumbo, marking the edge of an enormous ice-age lake. One can also take the trail off the backside of Mt. Sentinel, which zig-zags down crossing the parasailing jeep road a few times to a sign which shows the lovely trail down thru forest on Sentinel's north side that ends at the old railroad tracks, now the Kim Williams hike/bike trail, and then back to the parking lot at the "M" trails base. Doing the loop in reverse is also very pleasant.

see.name: Rattlesnake National Recreation Area
see.desc: There are more than 73 miles of hiking trails in the recreation area, many of which are also open to horseback riders, mountain bikers, and cross-country skiers.

see.name: Montana Snowbowl
see.desc: 950 lift-served acres at {{feet

eat.name: Greek Pastry Shop - #1 Gyros
eat.desc: Run by a Greek family, #1 Gyros can be quite crowded around lunch time. Tasty french fries.

eat.name: Bridge Pizza
eat.desc: Unusual pizzas sold by the slice.

eat.name: El Diablo
eat.desc: Another excellent burrito restaurant. The only burrito shop in town that cooks their meat fresh.

eat.name: Good Food Store
eat.desc: Missoula's answer to Whole Foods. Sells natural, organic, and specialty foods in its grocery store and includes a small deli serving prepared meals.

eat.name: Iron Horse Brew Pub
eat.desc: Modern restaurant with good American food that turns into a popular sports bar at night.

eat.name: The Old Post
eat.desc: Great food, great microbrews, great live music, and terrible lighting--this place has "atmosphere" written all over it. Excellent vegan and vegetarian dishes. Try the weekend brunch. The lunch-only "Reccession Special" is a local favorite.

eat.name: The Oxford Cafe
eat.desc: Diner style food in a business continuously open for so long that it prides itself on having lost its keys. Friendly staff, live poker, and cheap drinks. The chicken fried steak with JJ's gravy is amazing. Those looking for an authentic Missoula experience should check out this place.

eat.name: Taco Del Sol
eat.desc: Large burritos. Where many locals grab a quick bite.

eat.name: Taco Sano
eat.desc: Locally owned burrito shop, good combination of value and quality. Dubbed Taco Sysco, after the name of the food distribution company the restaurant gets its frozen meat from.

eat.name: Wordens Deli
eat.desc: Full-service deli, coffee, wine, and groceries. Missoula's first grocery store, Wordens opened in 1883 and has been a Missoula staple ever since. Wicked Philly is a local favorite.

eat.name: Black Coffee Roasting
eat.desc: Organic coffee from around the globe. Roasted locally.

eat.name: Drum Coffee
eat.desc: Baker making items in-house. Locally roasted coffee. Has second location at 1000 E Broadway.

eat.name: Liquid Planet
eat.desc: A very unique all-beverage store and organic coffee shop with a one-of-a-kind 10 foot high wooden globe that houses wine.

eat.name: Plonk Wine
eat.desc: A fun, delicious hip restaurant in an art-filled brick dining room. The roof patio is a cool and pleasant retreat on hot days. An extensive list of wines by the glass. Good vegetarian options.

eat.name: Bayern Brewing
eat.desc: Specializes in German lagers. Edelweiss Bistro offers food on-site.

eat.name: Big Sky Brewery
eat.desc: Distributes to multiple states. Their most famous brew is called "Moose Drool", but all are good. Visit the taproom for specialty brews not distributed elsewhere.

eat.name: Conflux Brewing
eat.desc: With outdoor seating, balcony views. Large space. Southern inspired food menu.

eat.name: Cranky Sam Public House
eat.desc: Fresh beers and curated wine list. 8 flagship beers. Rotating food trucks or bring in food from wherever. Live events.

eat.name: Draught Works Brewing
eat.desc: Local brewery making mostly ales. Also has rootbeer and ginger ale. Brewing is done right behind the main bar so patrons can watch. Has patio and features local bands.

eat.name: Highlander TapHouse
eat.desc: Outdoor seating right by Grant Creek. 12 craft beers on tap, live music, pizza.

eat.name: Kettle House
eat.desc: A much smaller neighborhood brewery, with excellent beers as well. Their Cold Smoke Scotch Ale can be found in most Montana bars.

eat.name: Ten Spoon Vineyard
eat.desc: A local favorite.

see.name: Whitefish Lake
see.desc: There is a state park and city beach on the shores. It is roughly 3300 acres and popular in summer for boating. There are public access boat launches, with a small marina at the Lodge at Whitefish Lake. The Lodge also rents boats and jet skis.

see.name: Stumptown Historical Museum
see.desc: Historical museum operated by Stumptown Historical Society. Learn about the logging and railroad industry and the impacts they had on Flathead Valley.

see.name: Smith Lake Disc Golf Course
see.desc: A huge 27 hole course. Major wind damage in 2021 has mostly been repaired but some upper holes are rough and missing signage. You will go into the gorgeous real wilderness on this course so: pack-in pack-out, be bear aware, bring snacks and water.

see.name: Whitefish Mountain Resort
see.desc: In the winter, offers a wide variety of Skiing and snowboarding terrain, from moguls to powder to bunny hills. In the summer, there's golfing, hiking, biking, and ziplines.

eat.name: McKenzie River Pizza
eat.desc: Gourmet pizza and pastas.

eat.name: Mambo Italian
eat.desc: Italian.

eat.name: Loula's Cafe
eat.desc: A breakfast option.

eat.name: Buffalo Cafe
eat.desc: A breakfast option.

eat.name: The Boat Club
eat.desc: Offers a standard selection of entrees.

eat.name: Tupelo Grille
eat.desc: Has a Cajun-themed menu.

eat.name: Whitefish Lake Restaurant
eat.desc: Offers a standard selection of entrees.

eat.name: Bonsai Brewing Project
eat.desc: Small batch ales. Kitchen with made from scratch comfort food, menu changes seasonally.

eat.name: Bulldog Saloon
eat.desc: Full bar with handmade burgers and other bar food. 15 TVs for all sporting events.

eat.name: The Great Northern Bar and Grill
eat.desc: Two full bars and a kitchen (consisting of burgers/sandwiches mostly). An outdoor deck is provided to allow for smoking, which is prohibited inside the bar. Live music three times a week, pool tables, shuffleboard and ping pong provide the entertainment. Usually is the busiest bar in town.

eat.name: Palace Bar
eat.desc: A small bar. A popular hangout for locals and those looking to escape the throngs, The Palace maintains a good crowd throughout the week.

eat.name: Remington Bar and Casino
eat.desc: Containing two full bars, it has two poker tables, shuffleboard and three pool tables. It also has the only dartboard (electronic) in town.

see.name: Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo & Aquarium
see.desc: This nationally renowned zoo is Nebraska's number one paid attraction. It features an expansive and aquarium, "Kingdoms of the Night" (world's largest nocturnal exhibit and indoor swamp), the Lied Jungle (world's largest indoor rainforest), and the "Desert Dome" (world's largest indoor desert).

see.name: Joslyn Art Museum
see.desc: Has works by El Greco, Degas, Monet and Renoir and an extensive ancient Greek pottery display. The Joslyn also has a glass sclupture by Dale Chihuly hanging in the atrium.

see.name: Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts
see.desc: A nationally recognized artist-in-residence program and art gallery that consists of three galleries in a warehouse-style studio. Tours are available by reservation and parking is free.

see.name: Omaha Children's Museum
see.desc: An art center, science center, and a mock grocery store.

see.name: Durham Western Heritage Museum
see.desc: A renovated art deco-style train station, it is believed to be the best example of art deco in the country with exhibits such as the Byron Reed Coin and Document Collection, the Trans-Mississippi Exposition Gallery, restored train cars, a teepee, an earth lodge, and more.

see.name: El Museo Latino
see.desc: A Latino art, history, and cultural museum. It is the first in the Midwest and one of 11 Latino museums in America.

see.name: Love's Jazz and Art Center
see.desc: Dedicated to the history of jazz, North Omaha, and Preston Love.

see.name: Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail Headquarters
see.desc: The National Park Service regional headquarters contains a small free visitor center about Lewis & Clark on its first floor.

see.name: Museum of Shadows
see.desc: A place for those who are a fan of the spooky, paranormal, or just plain creepy. Contains a collection of haunted artifacts from around the world. As a result, the building itself is now considered haunted. While there is no age limit, the owners state their museum deals with dark and mature themes and is not recommended for young children.

see.name: Malcolm X Birthsite
see.desc: His home no longer exists, but a marker stands on his former address.

see.name: Joslyn Castle
see.desc: It is the Scottish-Baronial style home of two of Omaha's most respected citizens and boasts four stories and 35 rooms. Tours are available to the public.

see.name: Mormon Trail Center
see.desc: It has various monuments, including part of the route the Mormons took. The site known as the Winter Quarters marks the pioneers' winter camp of 1846, and 359 Mormons are buried in a nearby cemetery.

see.name: Gerald R. Ford Birthsite and Gardens
see.desc: It pays homage to the late U.S. president. Twice destroyed by fire, the gardens stand where his house was.

see.name: Boys Town Visitors Center
see.desc: [https://www.boystown.org/about/visit/attractions#overlook-cafe Overlook Café] inside the visitors center is open M-Th 6:30-9:30AM, 11AM-1:30PM. The gift shop is open when the visitors center is open.

see.name: The RiverFront
see.desc: Urban park and greenspace stretching from 13th Street to the Missouri River, between Douglas and Farnam Streets. Completed in 2023, it replaced the Gene Leahy Mall and Heartland of America Park. Includes a concert/ performing arts stage, roller skate rink, and an observation deck with views of Iowa and the Missouri River. The park hosts concerts and plays in the warmer months and allows pedestrians easy access to the Bob Kerrey Pedestrian Bridge and Lewis and Clark Landing to the north.

see.name: Heartland of America Park
see.desc: Runs along the riverfront and has two fountains. The Heartland of America fountain shoots water {{feet

see.name: Memorial Park
see.desc: A playground, a baseball field, paths, trails, and plenty of open space. The park is unique because of its floral displays and historical monuments.

see.name: Elmwood Park
see.desc: Adjacent to Memorial Park. Has an 18-hole golf course, two baseball fields, a swimming pool, and many other things.

see.name: Lauritzen Gardens
see.desc: This {{acre

see.name: NCAA Men's College World Series
see.desc: Every June, the best college [[Baseball in the United States

see.name: Berkshire Hathaway Annual Meeting
see.desc: The so-called "Woodstock for capitalists", annually on the first Saturday of May, where investors all over the world come to listen to Warren Buffett. It might hold little interest to non business minded travelers, but just as important is that if you are not interested, better stay clear off Omaha during this period as the business crowd drives transportation and accommodation prices through the roof.

see.name: Orpheum Theater
see.desc: Built in 1927, this 2600-seat theater hosts Broadway plays, stand up comics, and musical performances. Parking is available to the south, across the road.

see.name: Film Streams
see.desc: Two single-screen movie houses showcasing lesser known films and foreign titles. One location is in the Dundee neighborhood and the other is near the baseball stadium downtown.

see.name: Omaha Community Playhouse
see.desc: Has a long and storied history as the nation's largest community theater. Marlon Brando's mother gave Henry Fonda his stage debut in the 1925-26 season. Community members and local professionals perform regularly in plays and musicals.

see.name: Shelterbelt Theatre
see.desc: An organization that produces new works by local playwrights.

see.name: Baxter Arena
see.desc: Opened on the UNO campus in October 2015 and replaced the Omaha Civic Auditorium (closed in 2014) as the city's main mid-sized indoor venue.

see.name: Holland Performing Arts Center
see.desc: A sleek, modern concert hall and home of the Omaha Symphony. Hosts events as well. Parking is available on the north side of Dodge St.

see.name: Lucky Bucket Brewery
see.desc: Offers tours of the brewery and a tasting room.

see.name: Craft Axe Throwing
see.desc: A destination for axe-throwing, tomahawk, and hatchet enthusiasts. Craft beverages are available. Groups and parties welcome. Experts will guide you through axe-throwing, ensuring a safe and entertaining experience for all skill levels.

eat.name: California Tacos and More
eat.desc: Specializing in fried "puffy-shell" tacos, this small taco place offers filling Mexican food, quick and cheap. Tables get scarce in the afternoon. Happy hour is 4PM-5PM.

eat.name: Chopsticks House
eat.desc: A small, family-run Chinese restaurant. Serves some more exotic dishes alongside the usual fare of Chinese food. Very friendly staff.

eat.name: Coneflower
eat.desc: Local artisanal ice cream. Offers both traditional and experimental flavors.

eat.name: Dinker's Bar
eat.desc: Since 1965, this bar and grill has been serving up high class burgers and beer. A great place to relax after a long day.

eat.name: Feta's Greek Restaurant
eat.desc: Serving homestyle Greek food. Gyros, kebobs, and baklava are all made in house. They also sell their in-house dressing at local grocery stores.

eat.name: Jade Garden
eat.desc: Chinese restaurant serving up a variety of traditional dishes. As of Apr 2021, take-out only.

eat.name: King Kong
eat.desc: Serves Greek food and is the home of the Triple-Kong burger. Free drinks with a student ID.

eat.name: El Pollo Tote
eat.desc: Offering breakfast and specializing in roasted chicken. An authentic Mexican experience.

eat.name: Los Portales
eat.desc: Authentic Mexican that caters to the more adventurous diners. Examples include steak served with cactus, quail, and tongue burritos.

eat.name: Runza
eat.desc: Home of the famous Runza sandwich, a Nebraskan staple.

eat.name: Spaghetti Works
eat.desc: All-you-can-eat spaghetti dinners, including garlic bread and salad bar, for under $10. Many choices of sauces and pastas. Full bar.

eat.name: Ted & Wally's
eat.desc: Homemade old-fashioned ice cream with several flavors and a menu that's constantly changing. Voted best ice cream in Omaha. Vegan options available.

eat.name: Valentino's
eat.desc: Great pizza and pasta for take-out or delivery. Many locations also have great buffets!

eat.name: Zio's Pizza
eat.desc: Uses natural ingredients and has huge calzones and great pizza.

eat.name: Avoli Osteria
eat.desc: A Northern Italian restaurant, located in the historic Omaha neighborhood of Dundee.

eat.name: Ahmad's Persian Cuisine
eat.desc: Great, authentic Persian food. All meals are prepared by the restaurant's owner, Ahmad, an Iranian immigrant. Located in the Old Market.

eat.name: Charlie's on the Lake
eat.desc: A lively atmosphere with some of Omaha's finest martinis, including the Pelini Martini named after Huskers coaching legend, Bo Pelini. Lush patio environment features breathtaking lakeside view and easy access to live duck sanctuary where restaurant owner Yves Menard gavages the stock. During summer months, patrons can select a duck and enjoy some of the finest foie gras and wine pairings in the Midwest.

eat.name: Hiro 88
eat.desc: Great Japanese restaurant that serves some of Omaha's freshest sushi and sashimi.

eat.name: The Jaipur
eat.desc: One of the few East Indian restaurants in the city. A modern take on Indian classics.

eat.name: Blue Sushi Sake Grill
eat.desc: Modern sushi with an energetic vibe, offers an extensive menu of raw, non raw, and vegan sushi, all paired with a collection of premium sake.

eat.name: Block 16
eat.desc: Nationally recognized street food. A large menus featuring juicy burgers, fried chicken, and poutine. Alcoholic drinks available as well.

eat.name: The Boiler Room
eat.desc: The Boiler Room is a hidden gem in the south side of the Old Market tucked in the gutted boiler room of an old warehouse. The food is usually sourced locally and has a heavy emphasis on gourmet French-style cooking, especially meat. Try the boar's head or scorpionfish. The menu changes daily.

eat.name: Gorat's Steak House
eat.desc: Favored by Warren Buffett, a dear friend of the family and a valued customer.

eat.name: Mahogany Prime Steakhouse
eat.desc: A great restaurant where you can get your fill on prime-grade steaks, Australian lobster, and Alaskan king crab legs. The food is amazing and they have a great wine list to complement whatever you order. Chain Restaurant.

eat.name: V. Mertz
eat.desc: An intimate and romantic ambiance residing in the Old Market. The menu, which changes weekly, is continental but also offers some innovative culinary creations from a range of cuisine types. Great for special dinners. Famous clientele have included Bono of U2, Warren Buffet, and Bruce Springsteen. Reservations only.

eat.name: Spencer's for Steaks and Chops
eat.desc: Aged, hand cut and seared meats. Featuring USDA prime beef from Stockyards Beef of Chicago, Spencer’s restaurant offers sizzling hot porterhouses, juicy filet mignon and the bone-in ribeye for which Spencer’s is named. Validated parking in the Hilton Garden Inn Garage. Reservations preferred.

eat.name: 801 Chophouse
eat.desc: A white cloth dining establishment in downtown Omaha. Offers lobster, American Waygu, and single malt scotch. Reservations only. Chain Restaurant.

eat.name: Hiro 88
eat.desc: Hiro 88 is an upscale Pan-Asian restaurant group. With the help of renowned architects like Japan’s Nakamura-san, restaurateur Milton Yin has created distinct atmospheres at each location, each inspired by its surrounding neighborhood. Serving Chinese cuisine and some of Omaha’s best sushi.

eat.name: The Crescent Moon
eat.desc: A large pub with a German Bier Hall down below. Checkout Max and Joe's tasting room next door. If you find a drink you like, stop in Beertopia to grab a six-pack of it, or any other craft beer you'd like, both owned by the same people. A must visit for all lovers of beer.

eat.name: The Homy Inn
eat.desc: Champagne on tap. This cozy bar is decorated with collectibles and memorabilia from yesteryear. Friendly atmosphere and a relaxed place to kick back.

eat.name: The Max
eat.desc: Ostensibly the region's largest dance club and gay bar. Two dance floors (electronica on one, hip-hop on the other), three bars, and a huge courtyard. On the weekends it's mostly straight people and expect a $5 cover.

eat.name: The Down Under Lounge
eat.desc: Eclectic bar with unique, quality cocktails. Be prepared to wait a few minutes while the bartenders mix them. Free live music W-Sa. Diverse and agreeable crowd. Before 9PM, order take-out from Mother India just a block west.

eat.name: Upstream Brewery
eat.desc: In the Old Market. Has pool tables and on Wednesday nights $7 pizzas and $2 microbrews are served. Also has a full menu and great food at a reasonable price. Try the sample platter of microbrews and get your favorite in a growler to go.

eat.name: Blue Line Coffee
eat.desc: Resides in a walkable area of Omaha, the Dundee neighborhood. Stop in and get "Green Beret", then walk down the block to 'Great Harvest' for a free slice of bread of your choice. Alternatively, walk west to the Bread Oven, a French bakery featuring traditional French breads.

eat.name: 13th Street Coffee Company
eat.desc: In Downtown, it serves a variety of coffee-based drinks. Desserts and sandwiches are also served. Occasionally there is live music on Fridays. Free wi-fi.

eat.name: Scooters
eat.desc: This fast-growing regional chain seems to have drive-up kiosks on every other corner, a testament to its popularity. Locations with seating offer free wi-fi. Original location is in Bellevue.

see.name: Lincoln Cathedral
see.desc: One of the finest Gothic buildings in Europe, at the heart of the medieval city. It was completed in 1092 but torn asunder by Britain's strongest recorded earthquake in 1185. Rebuilt, it became a great ecclesiastical centre, though the tower collapsed in 1237 and the spire in 1548. Notable features are the vaulted ceilings, the rose windows, the 1422 Medieval and 17th-century Wren libraries, the 18th century clock tower, and the baleful Lincoln Imp — look for him just left of the great east window. 21st-century repairs found that many flying buttresses had lost contact with the walls, so the cathedral was being kept upright by little more than the power of prayer, which perhaps has advanced since the last major collapse, and is another motive for the regular Anglican services here.
see.alt: Cathedral Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Lincoln

see.name: Lincoln Castle
see.desc: There's been a fort here since Roman times and probably earlier, but the stone castle was begun in 1068 by William the Conqueror. It has a large enclosure within its curtain walls, which from the 18th century was the obvious place to site a court house, jail and gibbet. So it feels Victorian or Georgian, though it holds an original copy of Magna Carta, and its most striking features are the jail museum and apparatus of punishment. The Crown Court is still in use.

see.name: Medieval Bishops' Palace
see.desc: This English Heritage building was built in the 12th century when the bishop was the temporal landlord of a great swathe of eastern England. It was ruined in the Civil Wars and never rebuilt; Victorian additions became a hotel.

see.name: Exchequer Gate
see.desc: Impressive 14th-century gatehouse by the cathedral west entrance. This was where tenants of church land came to pay rent — lots of them, for it was a big diocese. Their money was counted out on a chequered cloth, and "Exchequer" came to mean the government finance department.

see.name: Eastgate
see.desc: The 'east gate' of the Roman city of Lindum Colonia - a fragment of the 3rd century wall and gatetower are still visible

see.name: Priory Arch
see.desc: Replica stone arch - a reconstruction of the medieval stone gate which led to the cathedral close.

see.name: Lincoln Museum
see.desc: Museum purpose-built to exhibit the area's many archaeological finds. It includes the extensive Usher Gallery of art. The main museum is closed for refurbishment, but is expected to reopen at the end of 2026.

see.name: Museum of Lincolnshire Life
see.desc: Fascinating museum of the area's agricultural, industrial and social history from 1750, housed in a Victorian militia barracks.

see.name: International Bomber Command Centre
see.desc: In the Second World War, Britain's bombers were based across Lincolnshire. They took off at dusk and assembled in formation over the Home Counties, where they were joined by their fighter escort, and headed to targets. IBCC is a memorial and museum dedicated to all sides involved in this and later conflicts.

see.name: Ellis Mill
see.desc: A preserved windmill built in 1798, the last of the nine mills along the Lincoln Edge which ground corn into flour for the city. It's run by the adjacent museum but is closed to visitors.

see.name: RAF Scampton Heritage Centre
see.desc: This was the First World War RFC airfield of Brattleby, which returned to farmland in peacetime, then was re-activated in the 1930s. Early pilots used the line of Ermine Street to find their way home. Scampton was among the bomber bases - one famous unit was 617 Squadron, known as the "Dambusters" for their bouncing-bomb raid on the Ruhr valley dams in 1943. RAF Scampton is no longer active as an RAF base and has now been converted to a heritage site.

see.name: Mrs Smith's Cottage
see.desc: Mrs Hilda Smith cared little for modern frivolities. This mid-19th-century redbrick cottage got electricity in the 1930s but she held out against running water and an inside toilet until the 1970s, when the council were minded to declare the place unfit for habitation. Hilda died in 1995, aged 102, and the place has been preserved although the pigs have been banished.

see.name: Doddington Hall
see.desc: Grand pile built from 1595, the exterior is Elizabethan but the interior is mostly 18th-century. With extensive gardens.

see.name: Yarborough Leisure Centre
see.desc: Comprehensive leisure centre with gym, pool and athletics track.

see.name: Odeon Lincoln
see.desc: Large multiplex cinema with 9 screens.

see.name: Everyman Lincoln
see.desc: Luxury cinema with four small screens and sofa-style seating. Waiter service at your seat while you watch a film.

see.name: Lincolnshire Showground
see.desc: Large showground to the north of Lincoln hosting numerous events throughout the year

see.name: Lincoln Observatory
see.desc: The Lincoln Astronomical Society has public viewing nights in winter. In summer the evening sky is too bright.

eat.name: Bailgate Deli
eat.desc: Vegan deli serving coffee, sandwiches, salads and other light bites.

eat.name: Little Korea
eat.desc: Korean BBQ restaurant, also serving other traditional Korean dishes such as bibimbap and Korean drinks, both alcoholic and non-alcoholic.

eat.name: Hobbsons Pie Shop
eat.desc: Restaurant known for their meat pies, as well as serving local specialities such as Lincolnshire sausages. In a very historical building with famous residents including T. E. Lawrence.

eat.name: Gastronomico
eat.desc: Greek and other Mediterranean dishes - a little bit away from the city centre but has a great reputation amongst locals and with generous portions.

eat.name: Olé Olé Tapas Bar and Restaurant
eat.desc: Tapas and other Spanish dishes such as paella, designed for sharing. Very close to the west gate of Lincoln Castle.

eat.name: Slow Rise
eat.desc: Neapolitan pizza restaurant and takeaway, serving only vegetarian and vegan pizzas.

eat.name: Jew's House
eat.desc: Upscale cosy dining in one of Britain's oldest dwellings.

eat.name: The Old Bakery
eat.desc: Fine dining restaurant showcasing Lincolnshire produce. Run as a non-profit by Lincoln College, and used as a training kitchen and restaurant for advanced catering and hospitality students

eat.name: The Victoria
eat.desc: A city institution, this is a grand old pub with food and drink a-plenty.

eat.name: Strugglers Inn
eat.desc: A real ale pub, dating from 1841 and filled with brewery paraphernalia. The name comes from the nearby hangings that would occur at Lincoln Castle. Has a sun trap beer garden, popular during summer

eat.name: Magna Carta
eat.desc: Closest pub to the cathedral, overlooking the Castle Square. Very popular with tourists due to its location, with an outdoor terrace on the square and lots of seating

eat.name: Widow Cullens' Well
eat.desc: Samuel Smiths pub, so stocks the cheapest drinks uphill as long as you are fine with Samuel Smiths drinks. Very well-maintained historical building on Steep Hill. Has the typical Samuel Smiths rules (no phones, no swearing etc.).

eat.name: The Morning Star
eat.desc: Pub near the east of the Cathedral with very small rooms but an extensive beer garden.

eat.name: The Cardinal's Hat
eat.desc: Claims to be the oldest pub in Lincoln, and was first opened as a pub in the 1500s. The building was used as offices for a while but reopened as a pub in the 2010s, with a good selection of real ales

eat.name: The Treaty of Commerce
eat.desc: One of the oldest buildings on the Lower High Street - a former tea trader and became a pub in 1862. Now run by Batemans Brewery of Lincolnshire. Very popular with Lincoln City FC fans on matchdays.

eat.name: The Tiny Tavern
eat.desc: A micropub across from St Mary's Guildhall with a good range of rotating guest beers.

eat.name: Golden Eagle
eat.desc: Regency coaching inn, run by the Castle Rock Brewery from Nottingham. Has a good selection of ales and draught beers, and an expansive rear beer garden

see.name: Nevada State Museum
see.desc: Housed in the old Carson City mint with exhibits about the mint, Nevada and its people.

see.name: Nevada Governor Mansion
see.desc: Built over a hundred years ago.

see.name: Gold Dust West Carson City
see.desc: Hotel Casino with RV park. Casino portion features slots and sports book, no tables. Also has a 32-lane bowling center and restaurants.

see.name: Silver Oak Golf Club
see.desc: Exciting golf course in the hills surrounding Lake Tahoe.

see.name: Mills Park
see.desc: Large centrally located park with Summer kiddie train, skate park and events pavilion.

see.name: Fuji Park
see.desc: Large park with playgrounds, a trail alongside Clear creek, and an off-leash dog area. Next to fairgrounds and a fishing pond.

see.name: Washoe Lake State Park
see.desc: Just north of Carson City, this state park is a very good spot to view wild horses year round, as well as migratory birds in season. Popular area for windsurfing and paragliding.

eat.name: El Charro Avitia
eat.desc: Very good Mexican food.

eat.name: Cracker Box Diner
eat.desc: American breakfast open til 2PM. Does not accept debit or credit cards.

eat.name: The Fox Brew Pub
eat.desc: Old English-style pub that makes their own microbrews.

eat.name: Comma Coffee
eat.desc: Coffee shop that has a unique atmosphere with knickknacks, books, and artwork everywhere in a historic building with courtyard. Live music, jam sessions, and a monthly open mic. They serve breakfast, soups, sandwiches, organic coffee, Italian and French sodas.

eat.name: Tee Jay's Corner Cafe
eat.desc: Counter only seating. Offers a split menu of both American-style diner food and a selection of Indonesian dishes.

see.name: Museum of Nebraska Art
see.desc: Housed in a former post office, this art collection contains over 5000 pieces of artwork. The MONA celebrates Nebraska's artistic culture by highlighting Nebraskan artists like George Catlin and Robert Henri. MONA also hosts an annual Student Art Show in spring, showcasing works by budding artists from elementary school to high school.

see.name: The Great Platte River Road Archway
see.desc: Spanning I-80, the archway allows visitors to explore the settling of the west by the pioneers on the [[Oregon Trail]] and the construction of the Lincoln Highway. The audio guide is highly recommended. Outside the archway, there is a maze, picnic area, and a reconstructed sod house.

see.name: G. W. Frank Museum of History and Culture
see.desc: A historic mansion built in the 1890s by businessman G.W. Frank. After the Frank family left, it became a tuberculosis hospital for most of the 20th century. Walk-ins are welcomed for both guided and self-guided tours. Due to the age of the house and its status as a protected building, there is no elevator to the upper floors. A handicap accessible restroom is available on the ground floor. Operated by the University of Nebraska Kearney.

see.name: The Trails & Rails Museum
see.desc: An open air museum with eight historic buildings to tour, a barn, and a Union Pacific engine. Visitors are given a chance to explore life at the turn of the 20th century. Tours are available four times a day. The museum is run by the Buffalo County Historical Society, which has an archive located next door.

see.name: Nebraska Firefighters Museum
see.desc: A look into the history of firefighting, showing the changing technology and methods used to combat fire. The exhibits include interactive points, allowing people to participate in firefighting. The grounds also serve as a memorial to Nebraska firefighters who died in the line of duty.

see.name: Classic Car Collection
see.desc: A collection of 200 rare and classic cars covering the entire 20th century, including early motor buggies, 1950s Cadillacs, and modern collector cars. Combined with a collection of Americana along with it, if you're into classic cars this is a must visit.

see.name: Fort Kearny State Historical Park
see.desc: Established in 1848 to provide a safe haven for travelers on the [[Oregon Trail]] then abandoned and demolished in 1871. Now a State Historical Park with camp sites. All of the present buildings are reconstructions. The nearby State Recreation Area allow for boating, hiking, and wildlife viewing.

see.name: Viaero Center
see.desc: Home of the Tri-City Storm, the hockey team for the area. This event center has hosted everything from car shows, musical venues, and trade shows. If there's a concert in town, it's probably located here. Check the website for the list of upcoming events.

see.name: Big Apple Fun Center
see.desc: Bowling, lazer-tag, go-karts, and a sports bar. The entertainment complex also has a black light mini golf course. Each attraction has different hours and different admission prices.

see.name: The World Theater
see.desc: A volunteer run single-screen theater showing anything from old classics to modern television shows. The interior was designed to match the original 1920s style.

see.name: Kearney SportsPlex
see.desc: State of the art indoor sports complex with room for eight basketball courts, 12 volleyball courts, and over 60k feet of premium turf for soccer/baseball/softball. 4 pickleball courts as well. Very popular for youth sports tournaments.

see.name: Lillian Annette Rowe Bird Sanctuary
see.desc: This bird sanctuary covers over 2000 acres of land and becomes a prime crane viewing location during the migration season. The sanctuary also has prairies, wetlands, and river management programs to provide a safe place for wildlife. Tours are offered during migration season. Call in advance to schedule a tour.

see.name: Fort Kearny State Recreation Area
see.desc: This park is just north of the Fort Kearny Historical Park. Offering year round camping, fishing, and hiking, this 190 acre park shows off the beauty of the river valley. During the spring migration, tens of thousands of sandhill cranes rest in the sandpit lakes and the marshy lands surrounding them. The park includes RV hookups, showers, and a fishing pier.

eat.name: Angus Burgers & Shakes
eat.desc: Burgers, beer, and milkshakes. Offering Angus beef burgers sourced locally and portions to fill the emptiest of stomachs.

eat.name: Sakura Teriyaki House
eat.desc: Japanese restaurant serving sushi, spring rolls, and of course, teriyaki. Large bowls of rice.

eat.name: Barista's Daily Grind
eat.desc: A coffee shop offering a wide variety of blends, specialty drinks, and tea. Also serves pastries and baked goods. A popular place with university students. Offers catering as well.

eat.name: Bierhaus Maisschäler
eat.desc: German-style lagers, Bavarian-inspired food, and European cocktails. Burgers and other restaurant fare available as well. One side of the restaurant is a German Beer Hall, the other is restaurant. Full bar on both sides

eat.name: Nick's Gyros
eat.desc: Casual restaurant that sells burgers, gyros and other pita sandwiches. Live music on Thursdays. Cuts back hours during summer when UNK is in session

eat.name: Thunderhead Brewing
eat.desc: Serving their in-house beer along with a menu of pizzas, Thunderhead provides a good place to unwind after a long day. Happy Hour is Monday-Friday 4-6PM.

eat.name: McCue's Nebraska Taproom
eat.desc: Specializing in Nebraskan beer, wine, and liquor.

eat.name: The Dome Lounge & Package Store
eat.desc: Offers keno and pool. No food served but a food truck stops on Fridays. A hometown bar run by locals for over 30 years.

eat.name: NVY Bar and Cigar Lounge
eat.desc: Cigar lounge with an extensive whiskey collection. Cigar smoking allowed (no cigarette smoking inside), with outdoor seating available. Food trucks on site sometimes, with outside food allowed in.

see.name: Nevada Museum of Art
see.desc: The Nevada Museum of Art building was designed by Will Bruder and opened in 2003. It plays host to national and international touring exhibits in addition to smaller exhibits of regional significance. It is the only accredited art museum in Nevada. .

see.name: Wingfield Park
see.desc: '''Closed through summer 2026.''' Along the Truckee River just a few blocks from the casino core, Wingfield Park features an amphitheater with regular performances during the summer months, a kayak park open year round, and many pleasant spots to sit and watch the world go by any day of the week, at pretty much any time of the day. Home of annual events the [https://renoriverfestival.com/ Reno River Festival], held for three days in early June, and the [https://artown.org/ Artown Festival], July 1–31.

see.name: California Ave
see.desc: This area of small shops and restaurants is a short walk from the downtown casino core and provides a pleasant setting for a meal.

see.name: University of Nevada, Reno
see.desc: An ideal location for a pleasant stroll, the layout of the University campus was inspired by Jefferson's University of Virginia. Visitors will find a parklike setting with a variety of architectural styles, and the Fleischmann Planetarium. Guided walking tours are available by reservation.

see.name: Rancho San Rafael Park
see.desc: A few blocks west of the north end of the University, this 570-acre county park is home to an arboretum, as well as the Wilbur D. May Museum, a fishing pond and a large off-leash dog area. This is the home of the Reno Balloon Races, held in late summer/early fall annually. The northern half of the park connects to trail networks in the hills.

see.name: S Wells Ave
see.desc: A local neighborhood with a decidedly Latino flavor, this neighborhood features unique shopping and dining and generally winds down in early evening hours.

see.name: Idlewild Park
see.desc: A nice stroll from downtown along Riverside Drive, Idlewild Park features Reno's Municipal Rose Garden, as well as playgrounds, exercise equipment, a skate park, a swimming pool and various walking trails. On Friday evenings in the summer there are dozens of food trucks. Located on the south bank of the Truckee River.

see.name: National Automobile Museum
see.desc: You’ll see more than 200 eye-popping cars with authentic street scenes and sounds. The facades bring displays to life; a hardware store here, a movie theatre there which accompany artifacts from each era. Same day re-entry with receipt.

see.name: Terry Lee Wells Nevada Discovery Museum
see.desc: Children's museum with two stories of interactive exhibits.

see.name: Nevada Wolf Pack
see.desc: University of Nevada sports, competing in five men's sports, 10 women's sports, and one coed sport (rifle shooting), mostly in the Mountain West Conference. As with most major universities, the most widely followed sports are football and men's basketball. The Wolf Pack's rivalry with its sister campus in Las Vegas, UNLV, is especially intense. The main athletics venues are on campus, with the most notable being Mackay Stadium (football) and the Lawlor Events Center (basketball); the latter also houses the main ticket office for all Wolf Pack sports. The men's basketball team is planning to move to a new arena at the Grand Sierra Resort in 2026.

see.name: Reno Aces
see.desc: Minor League Baseball in the Triple-A Pacific Coast League, one of two U.S.-based leagues that are a step below Major League Baseball. The Aces are the top farm team for the Arizona Diamondbacks.

see.name: Reno Rodeo
see.desc: 10-day rodeo competition with championship events on the final day.

see.name: The Great Reno Balloon Race
see.desc: Three day hot air balloon event over Labor Day weekend. You can see the balloons from all over town once they are up in the air, but if you would like a good spot to see them inflate and take off up close you will need to get to the park before 5am. Parking can be a challenge due to closed roads; be prepared to walk several blocks uphill.

see.name: Hot August Nights
see.desc: Classic car show with free outdoor rock concerts.

see.name: Street Vibrations
see.desc: Twice-yearly motorcycle rally in June and September.

see.name: Best in the West Nugget Rib Cook-off
ARTOWN
see.desc: Artown brings distinguished artists from around the world to Reno each July 1-31, for music, arts and theater performances throughout the Reno area.

see.name: Circus Circus
see.desc: On the second floor, the circus acts and midway arcade are great attractions for families so if you're traveling with children, they should not be missed.

see.name: Club Cal*Neva
see.desc: This property features affordable gambling of all types and a variety of cheap dining options. This is the classic "Reno-style" casino and should not be missed, especially for those who like to gamble. For those who don't like to gamble, there are arcade games on the second floor.

see.name: Eldorado
see.desc: The Eldorado is a pink neon masterpiece featuring a variety of dining options including the Brew Brothers brewpub (with live music on Friday and Saturday nights), a steakhouse, a sushi bar, La Strada Italian Restaurant, and more.

see.name: Silver Legacy
see.desc: This hotel/casino was completed in 1995 and is the tallest building in Reno. It includes a cheesy "mint press" "churning out" souvenir coins as well as numerous dining options including several lounges, a steakhouse, coffeeshop, rum bar with dueling pianos, and more. Other features include a concert venue with frequent shows and a comedy club open Thursday through Sunday.

see.name: Atlantis
see.desc: This tropical-themed casino resort features a variety of dining options including an oyster bar, one of the last traditional casino buffets in town, and a steakhouse. Well served by the #1 bus. Other amenities include a pool, a spa and an arcade.

see.name: Grand Sierra Resort
see.desc: This is Reno's largest hotel/casino and the closest to the airport. The Hotel features nightclub with a pool and many decently appointed standard guest rooms. You will find a whole host of dining options including a Charlie Palmer Steak, Chickie and Pete's sports bar, and a buffet (Thursday through Sunday only). In addition the resort features the outdoor ''Grand Adventure Land'' (go karts, mini golf and a giant swing), a discount movie theater, an arcade, a bowling alley and a driving range. Well served by the #14 bus, though driving or taking a cab is recommended. In September 2023, the resort announced a 10-year, $1 billion-plus expansion that will add (among other facilities) a new 800-room hotel tower and a new arena that will host various events, most notably Nevada Wolf Pack men's basketball games.

see.name: Nugget Casino Resort
see.desc: This is a big hotel-casino/resort in Sparks' Victorian Square only minutes from the Reno-Tahoe International Airport. It features a great coffee shop, Rosie's Café, as well as The Steakhouse Grill, John's Oyster Bar, and Starbucks Coffee. Also regular live, weekly music performances from local and national touring acts.

see.name: Peppermill
see.desc: If you've been to Vegas and seen the Peppermill on The Strip, you might just have to do a double-take when viewing Reno's Peppermill. This is a large, well-appointed hotel/casino, with numerous dining options and a full-featured spa. Also South of downtown, well served by the #1 bus.

see.name: Basecamp
see.desc: This gym is part of the Whitney Peak hotel, but is open to anyone and is the only one in downtown. Basecamp has a small fitness center, 7,000 square feet of bouldering walls inside, and top rope walls on the outside of the building. Two of these top rope routes actually go up the whole side of the Whitney Peak building, making it the Guinness Book of World Records "World's Tallest Artificial Climbing Wall" at 164 feet.

see.name: Mesa Rim
see.desc: This is the newest and largest climbing gym in Reno. The place has bouldering, top rope, and lead walls, plus a fitness center and a yoga studio.

see.name: Rocksport
see.desc: The first climbing gym in Reno, this place boasts 7,500 square feet of terrain, 35 foot top rope and lead walls, and bouldering walls. All indoor, very family friendly.

see.name: Mt. Rose Trail
see.desc: Hiking to the peak and back is over ten miles (15 km) and takes a large portion of the day but rewards you with some very impressive panoramic views on a clear day. For a shorter excursion, the waterfall around halfway up makes a good turn-around point. Very good area for wildflower viewing.

see.name: Mt Rose
see.desc: The closest ski resort to Reno. This resort is at elevation {{ft

see.name: Heavenly
see.desc: Lake Views on one side (you're literally skiing above the casinos at the south end of the lake) and the desert valleys and pow pow on the other side. Huge amount of terrain and claims to have the West's largest snowmaking system for those dry years.

see.name: Sugar Bowl
see.desc: Two base areas with a little village in between and an extensive network of terrain.

see.name: Diamond Peak
see.desc: Ski right above Lake Tahoe on a well laid-out network of runs. They have carpetloader lifts, so be prepared for a strange boarding experience. Small resort, family-friendly.

see.name: Palisades Tahoe
see.desc: This legendary resort is home of the legendary KT22 and hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics.

eat.name: Peg's Glorified Ham 'n' Eggs
eat.desc: Peg's is always busy for brunch, but well worth the wait. A local favorite. There are actually five of these in Reno, the other four at 196 Lemmon Dr (North Reno), 6300 Mae Anne Ave (West Reno), 720 S Meadows Pkwy (South Reno), and 1495 E Prater Way (Sparks). The downtown location is the original.

eat.name: JJ's Pie Company
eat.desc: Sports, beer, pizza, and subs.

eat.name: El Adobe Cafe
eat.desc: Sit-down Mexican food. Family owned and operated.

eat.name: Miguel's (original)
eat.desc: Mexican restaurant that's been here forever (actually since 1959). Also family owned and operated.

eat.name: Miguel's (South Reno)
eat.desc: Mexican restaurant that's been here forever (actually since 1959). Also family owned and operated.

eat.name: Toucan Charlie's
eat.desc: All casino buffets in the area closed during COVID restrictions and most did not reopen. Of the remaining buffets, this is by far the best.

eat.name: Washoe Public House
eat.desc: Delicious American food. Vegetarian and vegan options.

eat.name: LEX Nightclub
eat.desc: LEX features three full bars, 33 VIP tables and deluxe amenities. The nightclub also features nine intricate skylights, a $2 million lighting system and an adult indoor pool partially covered by a glass dance floor, creating the illusion of dancing on water.

eat.name: Flowing Tide Pub
eat.desc: Locations on 10580 North McCarran Boulevard and 465 South Meadows Parkway.

eat.name: The Depot
eat.desc: Craft brewery/distillery and restaurant with 6 different beers 4 kinds of spirits.

eat.name: Great Basin Brewery
eat.desc: Brewery, distillery and restaurant.

see.name: Conway Scenic Railroad
see.desc: Enjoy the natural scenery of NH while enjoying a meal. Absorb the local history and check out North Conway station, in operation for more than 130 years.

see.name: Mt. Washington Children's Museum
see.desc: Offering activities for children and the whole family. Playgroups and birthday parties are among the museum's scheduled activities.

see.name: Mt. Washington Observatory
see.desc: The Observatory offers overnight educational trips, a pleasant view of the surrounding mountains, and guided snow tractor day trips in the Valley and up to the summit of Mt. Washington.

see.name: Foliage and Covered Bridges
see.desc: Old style wooden bridges and New Hampshire's scenic Kancamagus Highway of the White Mountains.

see.name: Cathedral Ledge
see.desc: Panoramic views of the Mount Washington Valley are accessed by car atop the 1000-foot tall (300 m) rock ledge. A very steep, easily driven road (Cathedral Ledge Road) leads tourists up the mountain in a matter of minutes where they are able to park and hike a 100 foot trail to the fenced viewing area. Easy access and limited area make this location slightly crowded at times. This area also attracts many experienced and novice climbers who ascend the rock face throughout the summer and winter months.

see.name: Attitash Ski Resort
see.desc: In the wintertime, Attitash offers 74 trails and Terrain Park for skiers and snowboarders. The Nor'easter Mountain Coaster brings you {{ft

see.name: Cranmore Mountain Resort
see.desc: Cranmore Mountain is a great beginner mountain, for those with small children learning how to ski or snowboard. It is a very family oriented resort, with a warm, cozy lodge. This mountain is also equipped for night skiing, with well lit trails for skiing or snowboarding during the night. You can rent skiing/snowboarding equipment from the resort, and take group lessons or individual lessons for beginners. There is also a tubing park located on the resort open until 9PM every day except Sunday, where it is open until 4PM. For a 2-hour tubing ticket, it is $23 for every age.

see.name: Saco Bound, Inc. & Rapid River Rafting
see.desc: Canoeing, kayaking or rafting.

see.name: Bike Shop
see.desc: Bike rentals.

see.name: Bob & Terry's Ski & Bike
see.desc: Bike rentals.

see.name: Outdoor Escapes New Hampshire, LLC
see.desc: Provides guided photo tours, moose tours, hiking backpacking, canoeing, kayaking, mountain biking, snow shoeing and cross country skiing.

see.name: New England Dog Sledding
see.desc: Dog sledding for families or couples that includes adventure and scenery (19min from North Conway).

see.name: Bretton Woods at the Mount Washington Resort
see.desc: Provides skiing, snowboarding, sleigh rides, dog sledding and snowshoeing.

see.name: International Mountain Equipment and Climbing School
see.desc: Rock and Ice Climbing, year round.

see.name: Ham Arena
see.desc: In addition to public ice skating, the Ham Arena offers ice hockey programs and figure skating practice ice for children and adults. The Ham Arena also features a pro shop stocked with hockey equipment, an on-site pizza and snack shop, and a video games area.

see.name: Northern Extremes Snowmobiling
see.desc: Provides snowmobiling with guided tours, canoeing and kayaking.

see.name: AMC Highland Center
see.desc: The Highland Center is a starting point for day hikes, paddling, snowshoe treks, skiing, and longer backcountry trips in the White Mountains.

see.name: Alpine Slides
see.desc: Mountain slides and water slides.

see.name: UberBlast
see.desc: Family fun with miniature golf, food and an arcade. Banana Village encourages birthday parties and summer camp group outings to their location as well.

see.name: Diana's Baths
see.desc: The series of waterfalls is very popular amongst tourists during the summer. Many come here to cool off in the frigid mountain water of Lucy Brook. A mild 0.6-mile hike from the parking area is required to access the falls.

see.name: Echo Lake State Park
see.desc: Good location for family swimming and picnics. A trail around the lake provides close-up views of Cathedral Ledge and White Horse Ledge. Pets are not permitted.

see.name: Mt. Washington Valley Winter Carnival
see.desc: Various events held around Mt. Washington Valley. Week long event typically held mid-February through early March.

see.name: Race to Beat Cancer
see.desc: Held annually in February to benefit the American Cancer Society

see.name: Mt. Washington Valley Winter Carnival
see.desc: Various events held around Mt. Washington Valley. Week long event typically held mid-February through early March.

see.name: Annual Taste of New Hampshire
see.desc: Chefs of the American Culinary Federation provide culinary and beverage demonstrations throughout the weekend.

see.name: Mt. Washington Road Race
see.desc: Held in mid-June, annual hillclimb up the Mt. Washington Auto Road.

see.name: Independence Day Celebration
see.desc: Includes fireworks around 9PM.

see.name: Labor Day Weekend Lobster Bake and BBQ
Labor Day Sidewalk Sales
see.desc: Back to school specials at more than 60 stores.

see.name: Fall Festival and Scarecrow Contest
see.desc: Held in late September through early October, free events for the whole family.

see.name: Fryeburg Fair
see.desc: A week long historical event only 20 minutes from North Conway held in the first week of October.

see.name: Fall Festival and Scarecrow Contest
see.desc: Held in late September through early October, free events for the whole family.

see.name: Polar Express Event
see.desc: This special event takes adult and children passengers on the Polar Express to the "North Pole" departing from the center of North Conway.

see.name: Hale's Location Golf & Country Club
see.desc: 18 holes. Par 36.

see.name: North Conway Country Club
see.desc: 18-hole par 71 course rated as one of the top ten golf courses in New Hampshire.

eat.name: Delaney's Hole In the Wall
eat.desc: Delaney's is a family oriented tavern with a variety of options on the menu serving lunch and dinner. Located in the heart of the White Mountain region in New Hampshire, there is always a crowd made up of skiers and snowboarders from all over in the winter. On occasion, there is entertainment at the restaurant, such as singers/bands. There are always TVs with sporting events on to watch as well. Their motto is "Big Time Portions – Big Time Drinks – Big Time Fun for the Whole Family."

eat.name: Horsefeathers
eat.desc: Horsefeathers is a great place for a sit-down meal. They are known for having excellent seafood. They do have a small menu, but every item is great.

eat.name: Moat Mountain Smoke House & Brewing Co.
eat.desc: Moat Mountain and Brewery is an excellent place for both children and adults. They have a vast menu that varies in price from $10-15. They are known for having some of the best ribs and burgers in the area. They offer five different types of their flagship beers and have over ten different types of seasonal beer.

eat.name: Peaches Restaurant
eat.desc: Excellent for breakfast.

eat.name: The Stairway Café
eat.desc: Excellent for breakfast.

eat.name: Peking Sunrise Restaurant
eat.desc: Lunch Specials daily 11:30-3PM.

eat.name: Black Cap Grille
eat.desc: Kitchen open until 10PM on weekends. Bar serves later.

eat.name: The 1785 Inn
eat.desc: At the Scenic Vista. Gourmet, innovative but casual.

see.name: Portsmouth Historic Dockyard
see.desc: A major naval heritage site within an active Royal Navy base, featuring historic warships including ''HMS Victory'' and ''HMS Warrior''. It also includes the National Museum of the Royal Navy and other museums, exhibitions and interactive attractions. Allow at least half a day to a full day depending on interest.

see.name: Mary Rose Museum
see.desc: The Mary Rose Museum houses the remains of Henry VIII’s flagship, which sank in 1545 and was raised in 1982 after more than 400 years underwater. The museum is built around the preserved hull, displayed in a climate-controlled environment alongside thousands of Tudor artefacts recovered from the wreck. Advance booking is strongly recommended.

see.name: Spinnaker Tower
see.desc: This striking and highly visible £21-million landmark tower rises some 170 m above the redeveloping harbour of Portsmouth, symbolising the wind filling a spinnaker sail. Visitors can use the tower to view from 3 levels: at 100 m, 105 m and 115 m. A high-speed internal lift takes you to the top.

see.name: Southsea Castle
see.desc: Built in 1544, the castle was part of a series of fortifications constructed by Henry VIII around England's coasts to protect the country from invaders. Heavily modified due to being in use until the end of World War II. Contains a rather random selection of cannon that have ended up in the collection of Portsmouth city council over the years. Has a small temporary exhibit with a permanent exhibit in the keep.

see.name: Southsea Seafront
see.desc: {{mi

see.name: Southsea Model Village
see.desc: A 1/12 scale village

see.name: Southsea Rose Garden
see.desc: Inside the 19th-century Lumps Fort.

see.name: Ernest Smith Clock Tower
see.desc: A beautiful clock tower over a barbers.

see.name: Portsmouth Cathedral
see.desc: A Romanesque Anglican cathedral in the old town. Contains a piece of Lord Nelson's flag and the tomb of a unknown member of the crew of the Mary Rose.
see.alt: The Cathedral Church of St Thomas of Canterbury

see.name: St John's Catholic Cathedral
see.desc: A Catholic cathedral in the city centre.

see.name: Royal Garrison Church
see.desc: A partly roofless English Heritage property. Only occasionally open to the public.
see.alt: Domus Dei (Hospital of Saint Nicholas and Saint John the Baptist)

see.name: Royal Marines Museum
see.desc: Covers the history of the Royal Marines. The museum is in what was one of the most stately Officers' Messes in England, built in the 1860s with beautiful ceilings, huge paintings and a grand staircase.

see.name: Eastney Beam Engine House
see.desc: Pair of compound beam engines built in 1887 to pump sewage.

see.name: The D-Day Story
see.desc: Tells the story of Operation Overlord during the Normandy D-Day landings including the Overlord Embroidery. Has an original LCT (landing craft tank) used at D-Day that has been restored and accessed by visitors.

see.name: Blue Reef Aquarium
see.desc: Take an undersea safari at the aquarium on the seafront.

see.name: Charles Dickens Birthplace Museum
see.desc: The famous writer Charles Dickens was born in this modest house in 1812.

see.name: Cumberland House Natural History Museum
see.desc: A fairly limited collection.

see.name: Portsmouth Museum and Art Gallery
see.desc: The Arthur Conan Doyle and Sherlock Holmes exhibition "A Study in Sherlock" is temporarily closed.

see.name: Portchester Castle
see.desc: About {{mi

see.name: Portsdown Hill
see.desc: Offers amazing views across Portsmouth and the South Downs. Just to the rear (north) of Portsmouth, it is a world away with countryside walks and traditional pubs.

see.name: The Royal Armouries at Fort Nelson
see.desc: Sits just on Portsdown Hill and is free of charge to visit.

see.name: Southsea Common
see.desc: Relax on the common with a picnic or barbecue.

see.name: Clarence Pier
see.desc: A small fairground close to the Hoverport with rides and amusement arcades.

see.name: The Bandstand
see.desc: Listen to live music here every Sunday in the summer.

see.name: Portsmouth FC
see.desc: "Pompey" play soccer in the Championship, the second tier. The women's team were relegated in 2026 and play down in the amateur tiers.

eat.name: The Tenth Hole Tea Room
eat.desc: Great for light lunch but the highlight is the amazing home-made cakes.

eat.name: abarbistro
eat.desc: Old Portsmouth. Modern European cuisine. Also great but you can drop a lot of money in this place, which has great service!

eat.name: The Beach Club
eat.desc: A relatively new restaurant right on the pebbles, with the most amazing views of the Solent. Great for a cold glass of wine, stonebaked pizza and pasta.

eat.name: Panero Lounge
eat.desc: British fare

eat.name: Becketts Southsea
eat.desc: British-inspired cuisine

eat.name: Bold Forester
eat.desc: Green King

eat.name: The Deco
eat.desc: Friendly rock and alternative, sometimes metal bar.

eat.name: Festing
eat.desc: Green King

eat.name: Hole in the Wall
eat.desc: Small pub with a traditional feel and real ales.

eat.name: The Honest Politician
eat.desc: A pub with pool tables and a relaxed atmosphere, and always a rocking soundtrack.

eat.name: The Wine Vaults
eat.desc: Good cask ales and great atmosphere, arrive early if you want a seat.

eat.name: Meat and Barrel
eat.desc: Meat majors on burgers, wings and ribs.

eat.name: Croxton's Kitchen & Tap House
eat.desc: Interesting range of summery beer. Food includes: Bavett of beef, mussels.

eat.name: The Lord Palmerston
eat.desc: Wetherspoons.

eat.name: Shenanigans
eat.desc: Irish pub doing breakfast and occasional music.

eat.name: Ship Anson
eat.desc: Green King overlooking the HMS Warrior.

eat.name: The Old Customs House
eat.desc: A traditional pub in a historic building, within a modern setting. Great ales and food.

eat.name: The Ship & Castle
eat.desc: In the ‘Devil’s Acre’ severing a carvery every day overlooking the HMS Warrior

eat.name: The Chambers
eat.desc: A plush pub with a roof terrace.

eat.name: The Dolphin
eat.desc: Claims to be Portsmouth's oldest pub.

eat.name: Spice Island Inn
eat.desc: Also has amazing views of the harbour in action and a good restaurant.

eat.name: The Still & West
eat.desc: A pub with a good view of harbour entrance and restaurant upstairs.

eat.name: The Wellington
eat.desc: The oldest pub in Portsmouth, established in 1710.

eat.name: Britons Protection
eat.desc: Behind the stage door entrance of the Bridgewater Hall. It is here where many a poor mug "took The King's Shilling" and found himself press-ganged into the army. Largest selection of whisky in the city.

eat.name: The Marble Arch Inn
eat.desc: Real ale brewed by their own brewery Marble and cask ale from micro-breweries nationwide.

see.name: Funspot
see.desc: Featuring the largest amusement in the state, outdoor mini-golf, an indoor golf dome, adult bingo, bowling, and more, Funspot seems to have an appropriate name. It is also home to the "Largest Arcade in the World" as recognized by the Guinness Book of World Records and the American Classic Arcade Museum.

see.name: Gunstock Mountain Resort
see.desc: While Laconia receives most of its tourism in the summer months, there are things to do in the winter, as well. One example is Gunstock. Gunstock describes itself as a "Four Season Resort," but their primary offering is its 1400-ft mountain (425 m), which is the second highest in the Belknap region, and completely ski, snowboard, and tube friendly. Gunstock offers a variety of trails with difficulties ranging from "Beginner" to "Expert," a fully stocked ski shop with rentals for those without their own equipment, and a lodge with several restaurants.

see.name: Laconia Motorcycle Week
see.desc: Although Weirs Beach is always busy during the summer, for one week, every year, "busy" is an understatement. Based around Father's Day weekend, "Bike Week" is the biggest event of the year in Laconia and attracts tens of thousands of bikers consistently. Bike Week is held at Weirs Beach, and attracts so many bikers and curious visitors that traffic in and immediately around Weirs Boulevard is completely closed off for the week. To attend, it's necessary to park in one of many makeshift parking lots and trek over to Weirs Beach, or preferably, ride a bike.

see.name: Weirs Beach
see.desc: In the summer months in Laconia, there is no dispute over where to find the most tourists. It is Weirs Beach. "The Weirs" consists of a boardwalk, which is about a half mile in length, a half dozen arcades, a pizza place, an ice cream parlor, an ample selection of souvenir shops, and of course, a beach.

see.name: Weirs Drive-In Theater
see.desc: Right next door to Weirs Beach Water Slide is the Weirs Drive-In Theater. While not particularly big, this drive-in always has the latest movies.

see.name: Weirs Beach Go-Kart Track
see.desc: Visitors in Laconia looking for a bit of speed may want to check out the Weirs Beach Go-Kart Track. People of all ages are welcome to ride on this quarter mile track. One seat and two seat go-karts are available. Group rates are available for those with 15 or more in their party. Ice cream and pizza is also sold here.

see.name: New Hampshire Pumpkin Festival
see.desc: The state's annual Pumpkin Festival I used to be held in [[Keene (New Hampshire)

eat.name: Tamarack Drive In Restaurant
eat.desc: Seafood.

eat.name: Tower Hill Tavern
eat.desc: Lakes Region's "Home of the Blues". Live music and great food.

see.name: Hudson and Manhattan Railroad Powerhouse
see.desc: The Powerhouse is a Romanesque revival industrial masterpiece built between 1906 and 1908. The Powerhouse was designed by architect John Oakman, an alumnus of the Ecole des Beaux Arts in Paris. The Powerhouse allowed the operation of the first trans-Hudson subway, the direct predecessor of today's PATH. It ceased operation as a power generating station in 1929. After years of neglect, it was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2001 after it was nominated by the Jersey City Landmarks Conservancy, an all volunteer not-for-profit organization. The city has designated the Powerhouse a developer, the Cordish company, which has renovated a similar power plant in Baltimore's Harbor.

see.name: Jersey City City Hall
see.desc: Completed in 1896, this imposing granite and marble municipal structure was designed by Lewis Broome, who also designed the Trenton Statehouse. A bronze memorial monument by Philip Martiny stands in the small plaza in front of the City Hall entrance. The memorial bears the inscription: "Erected by the People of Hudson County to Commemorate the Valor of the Soldiers, Sailors, and Marines of the Civil War." The statue is of the Goddess of Victory in a seated pose. Although she has lain aside her shield, her hand rests in readiness upon her sword, though she offers the olive branch of peace.

see.name: Justice William Brennan Courthouse
see.desc: This stunning Beaux-Arts style building is a glimpse into the county's rich and storied history. Be sure to check out its stained glass dome and detailed murals. Guided tours are available on weekdays.

see.name: Colgate Clock
see.desc: Dating back to 1924, the Colgate clock is a reminder of the numerous industries which once dominated the city. Manhattan residents still glance across the Hudson to tell the time from this iconic clock.

see.name: Liberty State Park
see.desc: Liberty State Park ([https://nj.gov/dep/parksandforests/maps/liberty-area.pdf map]) is as large as New York's Central Park but is far less developed. Nonetheless, it gets some 4 million visitors a year, drawn to the waterfront to see unsurpassed views of Manhattan, Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty. Don't miss fireworks displays over the water in the Fourth of July! Most tourists see the Statue of Liberty from [[Manhattan]], but if you're coming by car, it's easier to do so from the Park. Make your [https://www.statuecruises.com/ reservations online] ahead of time. Admission to the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island are free, but you must buy a ferry ticket to make it to both sites. The ferry is first-come, first-served, but your advance reservation will guarantee you a particular window of time in which to visit the Statue. Tickets are sold in the historic Central Railroad of New Jersey (CRRNJ) terminal. While you are waiting for the ferry to depart, be sure to admire its early 20th-century ironwork and architecture. For immigrants heading west to places like Chicago and Pittsburgh after processing at Ellis Island, this is where their overland rail journeys began.

see.name: Liberty Science Center
see.desc: In Liberty State Park. Home to the largest planetarium in the Americas, and it offers lessons on the biology of the Hudson River Estuary and an exhibit dedicated to skyscrapers.

see.name: Centre Pompidou
see.desc: Will open in 2023.

see.name: Loew's Jersey Theatre
see.desc: One of the five Loew's "Wonder Palaces," the Loew's Jersey was one of New York City's flagship movie palaces. The interior of the theater is surprisingly intricate and detailed; one person remarked that standing in the lobby of the Loew's is like standing inside a Faberge egg. It is being lovingly restored by a local group, and often hosts live events and screens movie revivals.

see.name: Lincoln Park
see.desc: Belmont Avenue at WestSide Avenue. In 1905, “West Side Park”, as it used to be called, was designed by landscape architect Charles Lowrie and Daniel W. Langston and features multiple historical points of interest. “Lincoln the Mystic”, a seated statue of the US President, was sculpted by James Earle Fraser. It was dedicated on June 14, 1930 when the park was given its current name of Lincoln Park. The fountain at the entrance of Lincoln Park was designed by the sculptor Pierre J. Cheronin and completed in 1911. It is {{feet

see.name: Apple Tree House
see.desc: House where Generals George Washington and Marquis de Lafayette dined and discussed war tactics. A walking cane that was made out of the apple tree that once existed is displayed in the Louvre Museum in Paris. Tours are available on Wednesdays.

see.name: Van Vorst House
see.desc: Oldest structure in Jersey City and one of the oldest in New Jersey. Build c 1740.

see.name: Paulus Hook
see.desc: Today, Paulus Hook is a charming neighborhood of Brownstone Row Houses with an excellent view of New York city, served by a light rail. It used to be a small peninsula surrounded by marsh, and connected the mainland by a causeway that was passable only at low tide. It was the main landing point before the Revolutionary War for travelers going into Bergen County from New York City. It has since been backfilled and Paulus Hook is no longer a hook. Paulus Hook was the site of British fortifications during the revolution that caused serious problems for the local revolutionary government- it was used as a base for loyalist raids into Bergen County. Major Henry "Light Horse Harry" Lee (father of the later Confederate General Robert E. Lee) took the fortifications by a night assault carried out during low tide on August 19, 1779.

see.name: St Paul's Roman Catholic Church
see.desc: One of the tallest and oldest church towers in New Jersey. Built in the 1860s.

see.name: St John The Baptist Church
see.desc: Designed in the 1890s with stained-glass windows, a Seth Thomas clock, a Romanesque-Byzantine edifice, and a recreation of Raphael's "Disputation of the Holy Sacrament". The church's design features a gold tessera (a fusion of pure gold leaf and two pieces of glass) which only four other churches in the United States have.

see.name: Pershing Field
see.desc: The park offers a lot of recreational activities including a running track, a pool, and an ice-skating rink. However, the park has a very deep military history since it was the location of a military camp during World War I. The park offers memorials for those who served in both world wars, the Korean War, and the Vietnam War. The park even has remnants of an old armory that once was located in McGinley Square.

see.name: Reservoir No 3
see.desc: This was the location of one of the nation's first water works facilities. The reservoir fell into disuse in the 1990s, and it began to look like a smaller version of the New Jersey Meadowlands. Today, the reservoir one of the few places within the New York metro area to view wildlife, but you must make an appointment online.

see.name: Empty Sky 9/11 Memorial
see.desc: Memorial dedicated to all 746 9/11 casualties from New Jersey. There are remains of the original towers adjacent to the memorial

see.name: Central Railroad of New Jersey Terminal
Skyway Memorial Park
see.desc: Memorial park under construction commemorating COVID-19 victims of New Jersey.

see.name: India Square
see.desc: Largest enclave of Asian Indians in the Western Hemisphere.

see.name: Ferry to the Statue of Liberty or Ellis Island
see.desc: Although most people visiting these sites take the ferries from Battery Park in Lower Manhattan, you can also catch the Statue Cruises ferries bound for Liberty Island and Ellis Island from Liberty State Park. The landing is directly in front of the old Central Railroad of New Jersey terminal building.

see.name: RPM Raceway
see.desc: Formerly the Pole Position Raceway, RPM is an indoor go-kart race track where you can race others at {{mph

eat.name: Wonder Bagels
eat.desc: Fresh bagels through the morning with a wide variety of cream cheeses and sandwiches available. As a bonus for vegans, multiple types of non-dairy/tofu cream cheese is available. On Saturday and Sunday morning, the line can easily be out the door.

eat.name: El Sason de Las Americas
eat.desc: Don't bother trying to speak English as, for the most, everyone speaks Spanish only. Pointing at what you want works, and the only word you really need to know anyway is ''pernil'', Spanish for pork. Super cheap and super good. They are located downtown at the intersection of Grove and Wayne Sts (a block from the Grove St PATH station).

eat.name: Ahri's Kitchen
eat.desc: Korean food.

eat.name: Dosa Hut
eat.desc: Although Little India abounds with South Indian restaurants serving dosas (a kind of crepe, made from rice and yellow split peas, usually rolled around a filling of potatoes and cashews), the Dosa Hut probably has the widest selection possible, with 30 dosas to choose from. Dosa Hut (as with many South Indian restaurants) is vegetarian.

eat.name: White Mana
eat.desc: (US 1-9). It has been here since the 1940s, and served up prize-winning hamburgers at the 1939 New York World's Fair.

eat.name: Taqueria Downtown
eat.desc: A basic taqueria with simple yet satisfying Mexican fare. This is not a typical "Tex-Mex" restaurant. The menu includes rules such as "no oversized burritos," "no guacamole," and "no fajitas." However, with tacos ranging from $2 to $3, you can easily have a cheap meal. Other basic and inexpensive Mexican fare is available.

eat.name: Little Quiapo/Philippine Bread House
eat.desc: Very cheap Filipino "turo-turo" (literally, point-point - as in, you point to the food you want to order) restaurants, while Little Quiapo is tucked away in the back of a shopping center. In front of the same shopping center is '''Philippine Bread House''', a decades-old baking landmark for Filipino pastries such as ensaymada, halaya, and pan de sal.

eat.name: Lee Sim's Chocolates
eat.desc: Locally owned chocolate store that opened in 1949. The customers come from around the US and the chocolate can be custom made.

eat.name: Second Street Bakery
eat.desc: A family-owned Italian bakery and deli.

eat.name: Kennedy Fried Chicken
eat.desc: Fried chicken joint handy to Journal Square PATH station, good for a quick bite before or after a night out.

eat.name: Razza Pizza
eat.desc: This restaurant is only open for 5 hours a day, and reservations and deliveries aren’t a thing here. The crowds, the long wait times, and everything else is all worth it however, as once you are seated you will get to taste some of the best pizza in the NYC area. Even the appetizers such as the bread and butter, as well as the meatballs, are worth the extra money. Some have even controversially dared to call it the best pizza in New York, including food critic Pete Wells writing for the ''New York Times''.

eat.name: Laico's
eat.desc: An out-of-the-way restaurant that serves some of the best Italian food in the NYC metro area. Don't expect to find anything else noteworthy in the area, but you will not regret coming to Laico's: the complimentary bread and house salad are enough to make it a worthwhile trip!

eat.name: Mamak House
eat.desc: Malaysian-Chinese fusion restaurant.

eat.name: Honshu Lounge
eat.desc: Ranked as the best sushi place in Jersey City by Foursquare and one of the 50 best in the United States by the Daily Meal.

eat.name: Cafe La Rustique
eat.desc: Great thin-crust pizza, among the best in town (try the mozzarella!), as well as quality salads and pasta.

eat.name: Rasoi Cafe Bar Restaurant
eat.desc: Their lunch buffet is fantastic. Service is spotty, but the food is worth it. Has been featured in ''The Star-Ledger'' (a local newspaper) and CNN. Also has locations in Edison and East Brunswick.
