Authentic and carefully prepared, don't miss the huge village platter (an appetizer that can be easily shared by two or more), gyros and well-spiced kebabs. Lots for vegetarians, and unbelievable sweet potato fries. Reservations only taken for 3 or more. On the weekends they're basically required, or you'll wait hours for a table.

eat.name: The Owl House
eat.desc: The Owl House has long been known as a vegan-friendly restaurant, although they do have non-vegan dishes. They will do what they can to accommodate any dietary restriction, particularly vegan and gluten-free. Even the brunch menu is predominately vegan and gluten-free; remarkable for a meal that often includes waffles and eggs. It's a tiny little converted house nestled in a row of bigger houses, so consider making a reservation. Outdoor patio is first-come-first served, weather permitting.

eat.name: Plum House
eat.desc: This popular Japanese restaurant specializes in sushi, particularly their sushi rolls, each of which has a rather unique moniker. The Yummy Yummy Roll is highly recommended, but you can also try the Red Dragon Roll, BFF Roll, or of course a Rochester Roll. Other typical Japanese-American dishes are available as well.

eat.name: Seoul House
eat.desc: Features extensive Korean menu -- Korean BBQ, scallion pancakes, spicy stews, etc. All meals come with lots of tasty extras, like fermented black beans and kimchee.

eat.name: Trata
eat.desc: An old military armory is the setting for this trendy hotspot that blends bar food with upscale entrees in a modern industrial setting. Everything about Trata is a unique mix of influences. There's a rooftop bar and some amazing outdoor seating available; inside there are more bars and seating across three floors of space.

eat.name: Whiskey River Pub and Grill
eat.desc: The former Steel River BBQ still has their popular smoked wings, but they've expanded into the historic building next door and now offer a variety of entrees in their dining room, along with classic pub fare in the bar area.

eat.name: The Distillery
eat.desc: Two locations close to the city and one in [[Victor (New York)]]. The food—including steaks—is hearty fare with decent variety and some international flavor.

eat.name: Jeremiah's Tavern
eat.desc: Originally a neighborhood bar on Monroe Avenue, Jeremiah's has since added some suburban locations. It's best known for its wings, but it also has a large menu of tasty entrees and sandwiches. In addition to Monroe Ave and Henrietta, there's one in [[Penfield]] (the Gates location closed but they're hoping to reopen in a nearby spot).

eat.name: Tully's
eat.desc: Upstate NY chain sports bar with an enormous menu. The real attraction is the chicken tenders and honey mustard which are nothing like the frozen variety served at most sports bars. There are dozens of televisions which makes it a good place to watch a game.

eat.name: The Alexander
eat.desc: This Victorian home has seen a sequence of restaurants fill its space since 1949, starting with what was once Rochester's most upscale restaurant, the '''Rio Bamba'''. This latest iteration has an airier atmosphere and a compact New American menu with fairly accessible prices. The Alexander is also aiming to provide distinctive event spaces within the building.

eat.name: Atlas Eats Kitchen and Bake Shop
eat.desc: While the Bake Shop offers light sandwich fare and breakfast dishes, the real attraction here for foodies is their Edible Atlas dinner series. Every two weeks, the kitchen selects a whole new cuisine to present to intrepid diners, be it Mexican, Korean, Greek, or anything else the chefs can think of. The menu is set in advance; all you have to choose is your beverage. You'll want to get reservations, though, as the restaurant offers only 18 seats for each dinner (one on Friday and one on Saturday). If you can't get a seat, try the takeout version (though you'll need a reservations for that, too).

eat.name: Avvino
eat.desc: An understated facade on busy Monroe Avenue belies the lively and slightly quirky atmosphere inside. (Check out the 18,000 pennies lining the floor of the lobby.) The food and service are top-notch, and the menu changes seasonally to incorporate local ingredients as much as possible. Mostly American fare with some Italian influences, like house-made pasta.

eat.name: Char Steak and Lounge
eat.desc: The Strathallan's signature restaurant is one of the finest dining options in Rochester. Upscale American entrees and steaks in a contemporary lounge setting. Breakfast is quite a bit more conventional to cater to overnight guests.

eat.name: CRISP
eat.desc: Texas-tinged upscale comfort food in an ultra-relaxed atmosphere.

eat.name: Good Luck Restaurant
eat.desc: Despite the name, this isn't some Chinese takeout joint. One of the most eclectic, see-and-be-seen restaurant/bars in Rochester. The menu is ever-changing, but a few staples are always there, including the full pound hamburger. Other options often involve rabbit, duck, and squid, to give you an idea. Even the more pedestrian options are made with high-end ingredients.

eat.name: Lento
eat.desc: With a name that means "slow", Lento prides itself on taking no shortcuts in the preparation of fine meals. Everything on the menu is made in-house, from primarily local ingredients whenever possible. (Check out the web site to see their list of local suppliers.) The care taken in preparation is reflected in the quality of the food.

eat.name: Max Chophouse
eat.desc: Not an ideal destination for vegetarians, this offshoot of the other Max restaurants focuses firmly on red meat, with a bit of seafood for flavor.

eat.name: Max of Eastman Place
eat.desc: Considered one of the top restaurants in Rochester, with an elegant atmosphere and a (French-inspired) menu to match. Popular as part of a night out at the Eastman Theatre.

eat.name: Next Door Bar & Grill
eat.desc: This restaurant is owned by Wegmans and showcases what Wegmans chefs can do. The menu focuses on sushi and seafood, with some land-based entrees as well, but it changes seasonally. The cocktails are something special and are made with the freshest ingredients possible since the flagship Wegmans store is located across the street.

eat.name: Phillips European
eat.desc: The food is only ok, heavy, traditional European—good for a business lunch or unadventurous out of town guests—but the desserts are ''spectacular'', with emphasis on pies, tortes, tarts, cakes and specialty cheesecakes. Examples include their Baileys and Creme Torte and Caramel Pecan Cheesecake. The mere mention of a trip here for coffee and dessert will get Rochesterians salivating. A full dessert menu is available in the restaurant, but the cakes can also be ordered whole and picked up.

eat.name: Redd
eat.desc: Rochester native Richard Reddington is a world-renowned chef, working in some of the best kitchens in San Francisco before opening his own restaurants in the [[Napa Valley]]. His original Redd earned a Michelin star for seven years in a row. But he closed that place in 2018 and returned home to open up a reimagined Redd here in Rochester. He's aimed for elevated cuisine in an "unpretentious" but energetic atmosphere—and largely succeeded, judging by the crowds. The menu is international in flavor but also includes his upscale versions of pizza and wings.

eat.name: The Revelry
eat.desc: Creative contemporary Southern/American fare in a very ''cool'' renovated industrial setting. Enjoy the lively bar and its scintillating decor, the breezy and fresh patio, or the somewhat quieter upstairs dining room. Not a place for comfort food; in fact, the menu occasionally errs on the side of weirdness, but it changes seasonally so it's always worth taking a chance.

eat.name: ROAM Cafe
eat.desc: A casual and cozy spot on Park Avenue for intimate Italian-American dinners.

eat.name: Rooney's
eat.desc: Nestled in Rochester's Swillburg neighborhood, near the Highland Park Diner, Rooney's doesn't look like much on the outside. Inside, though, is one of the city's best-kept secrets. Upscale dining in a rustic-romantic atmosphere makes this an excellent choice for anyone wanting to impress a guest. The menu is upscale American—veal, duck, lamb, swordfish, etc.

eat.name: Tapas 177
eat.desc: True to the name, Tapas 177 focuses on appetizers and shareables, but they also have a variety of entrees in the $30-35 range. On the drinks side, they specialize in huge martinis. The vibe promotes relaxation after a busy day at the office.

eat.name: Tournedos Steakhouse
eat.desc: One of the most expensive restaurants in the entire Greater Rochester area. The menu represents all of the high-end standards without going overboard on the creativity. The service is regarded by locals as impeccable. Lunch is a prix fixe three-course menu.

eat.name: Bug Jar
eat.desc: The walls display various works of art created by local artists, and the stage area/dance floor has an entire roomful of furniture arranged on the ceiling. Drink specials and live entertainment are featured here nightly, presenting popular local and national musical artists.

eat.name: Cheshire
eat.desc: This speakeasy-style bar serves up classic pre-Prohibition cocktails and inventive newly crafted ones with a sophisticated style.

eat.name: The Daily Refresher
eat.desc: The founders of this newspaper-themed tavern (with a speakeasy feel) call their establishment a "gastro-lounge", with a focus on custom cocktails and artisan foods.

eat.name: Lux
eat.desc: Lux is something of an alternative bar in Rochester and trades on being in the South Wedge to add cred to the atmosphere. Lots of tattoos and piercings and a good PBR special. The back yard is great. They have hammocks in the summer time and a huge wood burning stove for the winter. This place is something you would expect to find in Brooklyn not Rochester.

eat.name: Marge's Lakeside Inn
eat.desc: Once a speakeasy during Prohibition, this joint was one of the first in the area to get a liquor license after it was repealed. Today, it's a wild and raucous neighborhood bar; there's no food, but folks come for the drinks and the atmosphere. The deck extends out onto the beach for a great view of Lake Ontario. Parking is non-existent; you'll have to jockey for a spot on the south side of Culver. 21+ only.

eat.name: The Old Toad
eat.desc: Great English beer, poor English food, friendly English staff. A unique atmosphere with reasonable prices, the Toad is an excellent place to get sloshed.

eat.name: ROAR
eat.desc: Explicitly intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community, ROAR offers a surprisingly broad menu for an entertainment venue. But the real attractions are the performances. It's most well known for its frequent drag shows, but you might also find line dancing, dinner shows, or just a live band on stage.

eat.name: Turcott's Taproom
eat.desc: Turcott's Taproom is an English-style pub.

eat.name: Vertex
eat.desc: Goth/alternative dance club with a distinct no-judgement atmosphere. Come as you are, as long as how you are is ready to move on the dance floor. Generally a safe place for people who might get some side-eye out on the street.

eat.name: Wall Street Bar and Grill
eat.desc: You can get meals here—with waitstaff, no less—but the drinks are the attraction. In keeping with the name, drink prices fluctuate based on popularity, just like stock prices. Keep an eye on the price ticker; buy low and sell high!

eat.name: Rohrbach Brewing Company
eat.desc: Although Rohrbach's is a bit out of the way, their beer is worth the trip. Certainly the highlight is the Scotch Ale, and if you don't want to travel all the way to the actual brewpub, any number of establishments in the city will have it on tap, including Frontier Field. However, if there, do try as many of the beers as possible, as it is some of the best craft-brewing in upstate NY. You can get a sampler of {{oz

eat.name: Swiftwater Brewing
eat.desc: Great location in the South Wedge neighborhood just across the street from the Genesee River. Swiftwater is one of the most popular and fastest growing Rochester breweries. They typically have around a dozen of their beers on tap as well as a guest tap for cider. Like most breweries their focus is IPAs and they do them very well, but you won't be short on variety when you visit here.

eat.name: Flight Wine Bar
eat.desc: Dressy, sophisticated, and urbane, Flight might be the most well known wine bar in the city. As you might guess, they specialize in wine "flights"—tastings of a selection of wines based around a theme. You can try three different wines made from the same grape, or perhaps three different grapes from the same region. It's not just wine, either: cheese, chocolate, and even olive oil are presented in flights of three.

eat.name: Mullers Cider House
eat.desc: This cider-only bar has a dozen ciders on tap and over 100 more in bottles, as well as knowledgeable staff who can help you make a selection. As far as bar food goes, the house specialty is kettle corn, presented in seasonal varieties.

eat.name: Black Button Distilling
eat.desc: Black Button uses local ingredients to make corn whiskey, wheat vodka, and gin at their distillery. Tours and a tasting bar are the amenities available for visitors.

eat.name: Comedy @ the Carlson
eat.desc: The only dedicated comedy club in Rochester at the moment, tucked in behind Radio Social in an old manufacturing facility. Strong lineup of comedians, including occasional well-known national figures.

eat.name: Boulder Coffee Company
eat.desc: An independently owned coffee shop with regular live music. Their web page lists upcoming acts. Drinks and snacks are typical coffee shop prices. Free WiFi on the premises.

eat.name: Equal=Grounds
eat.desc: A coffee shop with a great open-minded atmosphere and an LGBTQ+ gift shop. The coffee, smoothies, and pastries are temptations. Grab a board game and enjoy.

eat.name: Java's Cafe
eat.desc: Another downtown coffee shop, more popular with the art house crowd, as well as those headed to (or from) the Eastman Theater. They also sell a variety of large homemade cookies in a variety of styles. At lunch time, an adjacent cafe-style restaurant serves for soup and sandwiches. Local art adorns the walls and local bands of questionable quality occasionally perform. Other locations at RIT and the Public Market as well as the YMCA in Pittsford.

eat.name: Joe Bean Coffee Roasters
eat.desc: A coffee roaster and full service coffee and espresso bar. Joe Bean has been mentioned among the best coffee shops in the country. They serve some food as well, but the real attraction is the java, which is fair trade and eco-friendly, and roasted right in-house. The focus at Joe Bean is on coffee education; they believe that good coffee can be savored and analyzed like good wine, and they even offer classes on how to make your own.

see.name: Saratoga Spa State Park
see.desc: Dubbed "The Public's Resort", this park has mineral baths, [http://www.saratogaspagolf.com eighteen-hole and nine-hole golf courses], free hardtop and clay tennis courts, and several pool areas with showers, locker rooms, rest rooms and food concessions. Hiking (and cross country/snowshoe) trails and picnic areas complete with grills are available as well. The park encompasses and protects the mineral springs in use at least as far back as the 14th century. This "Queen of Spas" was a 19th-century vacation retreat for the rich and famous.

see.name: Roosevelt Baths and Spa
see.desc: Despite the plethora of day spas around the city, this is the only place where you can relax in a natural mineral bath using water drawn straight from the ground. (It's mixed with hot tap water to bring it up to a comfortable temperature, though.) This facility was built in 1935 as part of the development of the park. While the mineral baths are their signature service, they also offer the standard menu of modern spa services: massages, facials, etc. The decor, with its aged porcelain fixtures and linoleum floors, may look a little institutional, but keep in mind any oxidation you see is natural, a result of iron in the spring water. And it's certainly the most authentic Saratoga spa experience you can get.

see.name: Frances Young Tang Teaching Museum and Art Gallery
National Museum of Racing & Hall of Fame
see.desc: A place to experience the history of one of Saratoga's most popular attractions, thoroughbred racing. Something for everyone with interactive exhibits, rare memorabilia, and equine art.

see.name: Saratoga Springs History Museum
see.desc: This museum is housed in an 1870 casino. It's not a must see for everyone, but if you are a history buff, and especially if you are from New York State or elsewhere in the region, it is very interesting to visit and a good value. A guided tour of the ground floor is included in your admission and adds a lot of context and value to your visit. Allow 2 hours or so to see the rooms; the artifacts from the casino and the grand hotels that served visitors to this town in its 19th-to-early 20th-century heyday before being torn down in the 1950s; information about some very notable citizens of Saratoga including the remarkable woman who founded the Daughters of the American Revolution, replete with documentation and their personal effects; and an exhibit about the Native tribes who inhabited the area. The staff are very happy to speak with visitors and share information, even at closing time.

see.name: Yaddo Gardens
see.desc: Artist community on a 400-acre site.

see.name: Adirondack Balloon Flights
see.desc: Enjoy the gorgeous views of the Adirondack Region and the Green Mountains of Vermont from high in the sky with an experienced ballooning crew.

see.name: Caffè Lena
see.desc: Acoustic music in a 110-seat coffeehouse that opened in 1960. The venue enjoys a world-wide reputation for preserving and furthering American musical traditions. Its archives are held at the American Folklife Center at the Library of Congress. The schedule features a mix of established career musicians and nationally touring emerging artists. Emerging artists presented by Caffe Lena have included Bob Dylan, EmmyLou Harris, Don McLean, Arlo Guthrie, Ani DiFranco, G. Love and Sawyer Fredericks. A complete performer list dating back to May 21, 1960 can be viewed on the venue's website. Hospitality for concert-goers includes desserts, light fare, local craft beer, wine, coffees and teas. The venue is operated as a non-profit organization.

see.name: Saratoga Performing Arts Center
see.desc: Summer home of the New York City Ballet, the Philadelphia Orchestra and various concerts such as the Dave Matthews Band.

see.name: Saratoga Casino Hotel
see.desc: Harness racing and video gaming.

see.name: Saratoga Race Course
see.desc: Thoroughbred horse racing from late July to early September.

see.name: Saratoga Lake Golf Club
see.desc: Eighteen holes with lots of up/down.

see.name: Saratoga National Golf Club
see.desc: Named 2005 "Golf Course of the Year" by National Golf Course Owners Association. Named "One of America's 100 Greatest Public Courses 2005-2006" by Golf Digest.

see.name: Saratoga Spa Golf Course
see.desc: Towering pines surround this 7,100-yard course.

see.name: Flurry Festival
see.desc: More than 5000 attendees flock to the city for the annual Flurry Festival, which features folk dance and music, including one of the largest contra dances in the U.S.

eat.name: Bruno's Restaurant
eat.desc: Check out the famous wood-fired pizza and homemade soups.

eat.name: Char Koon
eat.desc: If you're in the mood for Chinese, look no further than this delicious spot downtown. Good price, great food, and also serves Thai.

eat.name: Chez Sophie Bistro
eat.desc: Upscale French bistro located at The Saratoga.

eat.name: Compton's
eat.desc: Early morning breakfast. Opens when the bars close.

eat.name: Forno Bistro
eat.desc: Though styled a "rustic, Tuscan-style" bistro on their website, it seems much more Italian-American, based on its menu and portions. Either way, the food is delicious, the wine list is excellent, the service is really helpful and considerate, and this big eating hall is so popular with locals that you should expect to wait 20-30 minutes for a table for two on any given Tuesday if you arrive without reservations. Don't be surprised if there are two receptions in different parts of the restaurant, and wait if you need to. There are two outdoor eating areas on patios, in addition to inside dining, and they are heated on chilly nights.

eat.name: Four Seasons Natural Food Store & Cafe
eat.desc: This vegetarian spot has a variety of soups, salads, and hot en trees. While you are there, check out the retail store which offers a selection of natural foods, teas, supplements, and personal care and organic produce.

eat.name: Gaffney's Restaurant
eat.desc: Great courtyard dining during track season, indoor and pub dining available.

eat.name: Hattie's Restaurant
eat.desc: "Hattie" may have long since passed, but her Cajun tastes are still reflected on the menu, which includes her signature fired chicken.

eat.name: Longfellows Hotel, Restaurant & Conference Center
eat.desc: Good location for weddings, businesses meetings or private gatherings.

eat.name: The Merry Monk Restaurant and Bar
eat.desc: Classic bistro decor makes this a great spot for cocktails or dinner. Ask for a corner banquette table to enjoy a cozy meal for two and listen to the funky world beat soundtrack.

eat.name: Mexican Connection
eat.desc: Viva De Mexico, best mex going! Away from downtown but near the track.

eat.name: Mouzon House
eat.desc: Located in a renovated Victorian house, this sister restaurant to One Caroline Street Bistro specializes in locally-sourced cuisine with a Cajun flair. Try the Crawfish Beignets!

eat.name: The Olde Bryan Inn
eat.desc: 18th-century inn.

eat.name: One Caroline Street Bistro
eat.desc: Jazz with dinner, reservations or wait required but worth it.

eat.name: Panza's Restaurant
eat.desc: Enduring Italian restaurant serving classics such as parmigiana, pasta & steaks.

eat.name: Pennell's Restaurant
eat.desc: Family-owned Italian restaurant.

eat.name: Pizza Works
eat.desc: Pizzaworks is a family pizzeria. Their hand-tossed New York-style, thin-crust pizza is based on a traditional Italian family recipe. They also serve a variety of subs, wings, calzones, stromboli, wraps, salads and appetizers including bread sticks and garlic knots.

eat.name: PJ's Bar-B-QSA
eat.desc: South Broadway (US Route 9). Barbecue chicken and ribs; includes two 20-foot barbecue pits out in the back. Located about one mile from the Northway, open year-round.

eat.name: Putnam Market
eat.desc: Specialty food store and deli.

eat.name: Sushi Thai Garden
eat.desc: Light eating.

eat.name: Saratoga City Tavern
eat.desc: Pub fare.

eat.name: Spring Street Deli
eat.desc: Neighborhood delicatessen, featuring sandwiches named for famous thoroughbred race horses.

eat.name: Uncommon Grounds
eat.desc: Serves coffee, bagels, bagel sandwiches and such. A local favorite.

eat.name: Wheatfields Restaurant and Bar
eat.desc: Pasta, steak, etc.

eat.name: Desperate Annie's
eat.desc: A Caroline Street institution since who-knows-when.

eat.name: The Merry Monk
eat.desc: Classic bistro decor makes this a great spot for cocktails or dinner.

eat.name: The Parting Glass
eat.desc: This local favorite had tons to offer, live music and great food add to the appeal of this one of a kind bar.

eat.name: Tin 'n' Lint
eat.desc: A 1930s-era saloon.

eat.name: Trotters
eat.desc: A great place to watch football on Sundays, or start out your night. Inexpensive and the best specials in town.

see.name: Albany City Hall
see.desc: Designed by renowned architect H.H. Richardson in the Romanesque style he popularized.

see.name: Empire State Plaza
see.desc: The Empire State Plaza is something to behold. It lies between the New York State Capitol building and the New York State Museum. While many critics have found that the Plaza is architecturally intimidating, at best, it can be quite beautiful. Free concerts are often held on the plaza during the summer, ranging from Blues Festivals to Rock concerts. And the Fourth of July fireworks are spectacular.

see.name: New York State Capitol
see.desc: Free guided tours, M-F 10AM, noon, 2PM, and 3PM; Sa & Su 11AM, 1PM, and 3PM. Free self-guided audio tours M-F, 9AM-3PM (driver license or passport must be left as collateral for audio player). Plaza Visitor Center, Rm. 106 Concourse, Empire State Plaza. Security screening will confiscate pocket knives and other sharp objects.

see.name: New York State Education building
see.desc: Impressive neo-classical colonnade.

see.name: State Street
see.desc: The main street that runs to the Albany Waterfront. Though much of the lower portion is decayed and empty, it retains a regal air and is well worth a visit, particularly as revitalization of the area takes hold. State Street is home to many of the stately 19th-century homes that can be seen in Albany and was once home to writer Herman Melville. Nearby lies Pearl Street, which has undergone a renewal, and which caters to the 20-something bar and club scene. During the summer, the Alive at 5 concert series is an open festival on Broadway near the base of State Street. It draws quite a large crowd, and is generally a fun time for all. You can no longer bring your own beer, however—you must purchase it on site.

see.name: State University of New York (SUNY) System Administration Building
see.desc: Formerly the [http://www.albany.edu/museum/wwwmuseum/statestreet/dhbuild.html Delaware and Hudson Railroad Building]

see.name: Van Ostrande-Radliff House
see.desc: Built circa 1728, it is the oldest remaining Dutch building in the city.

see.name: Corning Tower Observation Deck
see.desc: The view from the 42nd floor '''Corning Tower Observation Deck''' encompasses not only the city of Albany but the foothills of the [[Adirondacks]], the [[Catskills]], and the [[Berkshires]] of western Massachusetts. Check-in at the security desk in the concourse under the Corning Tower, photo ID required. Plaza information office.

see.name: USS Slater (DE-766)
see.desc: Retired World War II US Navy Destroyer Escort, offering tours W-Su during the summer. Recommended ability to climb and descend stairs.

see.name: New York State Museum
see.desc: The largest state museum in all the 50 states, has some really nice collections.

see.name: Albany Institute of History and Art
see.desc: Another nice museum well worth a visit.

see.name: Shaker Heritage Society
see.desc: Watervliet was the first Shaker community in the United States. Shaker leader Ann Lee is buried here. Guided tours June through October, Sa at 11:30AM and 1:30PM, when available. Other tours available by appointment; two weeks notice required. See other Shaker villages in the northeast United States through the itinerary [[Touring Shaker country]].

see.name: Washington Park
see.desc: A delightful, and for the most part safe, park (care should be taken at night). In the park's center is the ''Park Playhouse'', which offers free, good musicals and plays throughout the summer. May offers "Tulip Fest" a nod to Albany's Dutch heritage that consumes Washington Park with (mostly) tulips as well as a craft fair.

see.name: Lark Street
see.desc: A center of Albany youth culture and an interesting place to visit. Lark Street is between Washington Park and the Empire State Plaza and is the main drag for a vibrant residential neighborhood. In September, Lark Street hosts one of Albany's most treasured events, "Larkfest", a popular street fair.

see.name: Albany Pine Bush Preserve
see.desc: Western edge of the city. It's a 3,000-acre inland pine barren maintained by controlled fires (which clear out invasive plant species and cause the native pine cones to release their seeds). Trails through the preserve are open to non-motorized uses year-round (except during burns, of course

see.name: Public concerts
see.desc: Held at the Empire State Plaza, Washington park and in the Corning Preserve/Albany Riverfront Park on the Hudson River during the summer.

see.name: Playhouse
see.desc: Plays held at the park playhouse during the Summer.

see.name: First Fridays
see.desc: Held every First Friday of the month, this event aims to bring to a wider audience the local artists and local shops of Albany. Artwork exhibitions, live entertainment and gallery openings bring Albany to life. For transportation; A trolley will stop at participating venues throughout Albany. The trolley leaves from the Upstate Artists Guild at 5PM and duration of the round trip is approximately 30 minutes. After the First Friday event, live music and original films are played from the Capitol Region Film Makers and people dancing.

see.name: Mohawk Hudson-River Bikeway
see.desc: A 86-mile-long trail for biking, walking, jogging or skating which starts in the Corning Preserve in downtown Albany, right along the Hudson River, and stretches out to Rotterdam Junction in Schenectady County.

see.name: Corning City Preserve
see.desc: Trails for biking, skating, jogging and walking in the 5-mile long park along the Hudson River, with picnic areas and a boat launch.

see.name: Albany Firebirds
see.desc: The Firebirds are Albany's professional arena football team. They compete in the Arena Football League (AFL). The Firebirds play their games at the Times Union Center. Tickets range in price from $10-35.

see.name: Albany Patroons
see.desc: The Albany Patroons play in the Continental Basketball Association (CBA). The Patroons play at the Washington Avenue Armory. Tickets range in price from $7-52.

see.name: Albany Devils
see.desc: The Albany Devils are the professional hockey team of Albany. They play in the American Hockey League (AHL).

see.name: Tri-City Valleycats
see.desc: The Valleycats are nearby Troy's minor league baseball team. The team is an independent team that competes in the Frontier League (it was in the New York-Penn League until 2019 and was at the time associated with the Houston Astros, but the NYPL was dissolved when the minor leagues were reorganized before the 2021 season). The Valleycats play at Joseph L. Bruno Stadium. Tickets range in price from $5–15.

see.name: Albany Great Danes
see.desc: Sports teams of the University at Albany (locally called UAlbany), competing in 8 men's sports and 10 women's sports, mostly in the America East Conference. The football team plays in FCS, the second level of D-I football, in the Colonial Athletic Association. Most venues are on campus, with the highest-profile ones being Casey Stadium (football) and SEFCU Arena (basketball).

see.name: Capital Repertory Theatre
see.desc: N. Pearl St.

see.name: The Egg
see.desc: Downtown.

see.name: The Times Union Arena
see.alt: formerly the Pepsi Arena and Knickerbocker Arena

see.name: Pick apples
see.desc: Autumn is always a good time for apple-picking at any one of the orchards in the area

see.name: Ice-skating
see.desc: The reflecting pool of the '''Empire State Plaza''' becomes a skating rink during the winter, which might be an equivalent of the Rockefeller Center rink.

see.name: Captain JP Cruise Line
see.desc: The Captain JP can accommodate up to 600 passengers and is by far the most lavish vessel in the Capital District. The Capt. JP II has three climate-controlled enclosed decks, along with full service bars and dance floors on each deck. They regularly feature live entertainment on the music cruises and also hold private events.

see.name: The Linda - WAMC's Performing Arts Studio
see.desc: The Linda is on Central Avenue in Albany. Visit the venue for many kinds of events or rent out the space for your own event

see.name: Huck Finn's Playland
see.desc: small amusement park designed for younger ages primarily.

see.name: Tulip Festival
see.desc: Showcases the beauty of American tulips, and not to mention the feast on food and art.

see.name: Capital District Scottish Games
see.desc: Scottish culture get showcased this time of year from pipes and drum bands to feasting and drinking over Scottish delights or just viewing an exhibition of horses, going back to your routes through genealogy information or maybe getting fashionable through tradition Scottish clothing. Though far from Scotland, this festival might give you an introduction to what your next destination may like be.

see.name: The Albany Chefs' Food & Wine Festival
see.desc: Regional chefs, restaurants, wines and beers.

eat.name: Cafe Cappriccio
eat.desc: An upscale NYC-Style restaurant. Wonderful staff, beautiful live jazz. Dress accordingly, you won't be disappointed.

eat.name: Fresh N' Pressed
eat.desc: Superb for healthful, super tasty and interesting sandwiches and wraps. Beautiful desserts to tempt you if you have room after their generous salads and sandwiches. Highly recommended, an outstanding value.

eat.name: El Loco
eat.desc: A good Mexican restaurant, loved by locals. The food can sometimes be a bit expensive for what's being offered.

eat.name: El Mariachi
eat.desc: Authentic Mexican cooking. It's not expensive, and the food is exquisite. Recommended!

eat.name: Gandhi
eat.desc: Indian restaurant boasts the best weekday lunch buffet in the area.

eat.name: Jack's Oyster House
eat.desc: An Albany classic, its walls are adorned with misty photos of Albany's interesting past. The quality and prestige of Jack's has gone down, though it still may be the best place to get fresh seafood at a place that has defined downtown for almost one hundred years. Don't dress like a slob.

eat.name: Mamoun's
eat.desc: A wonderful Middle Eastern restaurant. The dim lighting and brick walls gives this place a unique classy atmosphere. Food is healthy and reasonably priced.

eat.name: Wolff's Biergarten
eat.desc: Wolff's offers authentic German food and beer selections and there is always a futball game on.

eat.name: Honest Weight Food Co-op
eat.desc: For health food shopping, has a variety of health-minded dishes and baked goods made daily. Grab a "meal deal" for under $5. Check out the amazing cheese selection.

eat.name: Cafe Italia
eat.desc: An upscale Italian restaurant.

eat.name: Junior's
eat.desc: A good bar and restaurant. Many will argue their wings (as opposed to Wings Over) are the best in the city. Great burgers and grilled sandwiches.

eat.name: Cafe Madison
eat.desc: This is a wonderful restaurant that serves a brunch that is unparalleled in the capital region. Enjoyable patio dining is available during the warm months. Try their breakfast cocktails (their bloody mary is unmatched.) Part of the menu is on a weekly rotation which features creative takes on eggs benedict.

eat.name: Pepper Jack's
eat.desc: Pepper Jack's has a large variety of inexpensive delicious food. College students and professionals alike love this place. Try their breakfast wraps, simply amazing!

eat.name: Mr. Pio Pio
eat.desc: Columbian and Ecuadorian cuisine.

eat.name: Ragonese Italian Imports
eat.desc: This is an excellent Italian and Greek deli. You can get sandwiches, subs, soups, and even lasagne. There isn't really any place to sit down, so virtually every customer gets take-out.

eat.name: Salsa Latina Restaurant
eat.desc: A well-established Mexican restaurant. Great food, worth a visit.

eat.name: Swifty's
eat.desc: They have really good Irish and American pub food. Very relaxed professional and working class crowd.

eat.name: Karavalli Restaurant
eat.desc: For spicy south India cuisine, this is a nice place to visit. Many will say the atmosphere is lacking but the food will keep you coming back.

eat.name: Koto Japanese Steak House
eat.desc: A hibachi (teppan-style cooking) and sushi restaurant located right by Albany Airport, and is probably the most popular of its kind in the area.

eat.name: Peaches Cafe
eat.desc: A local favorite, reasonably priced and has excellent breakfast food. Try their Irish Eggs Benedict. Careful, this place can be very busy around lunchtime or weekend mornings, although weekdays aren't too crazy.

eat.name: Professor Java's Coffee Sanctuary
eat.desc: This is a wonderful cafe and a local favorite. Great atmosphere, the walls are filled with photography or paintings from local artists, all of which are available for sale. The food is excellent. The baked goods are divine. And their coffee and tea selection is endless. Try the Russian Caravan Tea if you dare! Java's typically hosts the indie-college crowd, many of whom come here to write papers and leech off their free Wifi. Very friendly staff. Sometimes, Java's hosts open-mic nights.

eat.name: Saati Deli and Catering
eat.desc: Excellent homemade salads, soups and sandwiches. Prices are comparable to places like Panera Bread, but you have much better atmosphere and quality here.

eat.name: Smokey Bones BBQ & Grill
eat.desc: Large place with plenty of TVs for watching whatever sporting event happens to be on.

eat.name: Sushi Tei
eat.desc: An excellent place with wonderful food and a relaxed atmosphere. Serve lunch and dinner. Many different choices of sushi and Japanese dishes.

eat.name: Oh Bar
eat.desc: A popular gay and lesbian bar that is friendly and has a nice happy hour. Check out Karaoke night on Thursdays.

eat.name: The Lionheart
eat.desc: Good on weekends when the Romans come down for their orgy, good happy hour specials, a good selection of beer, and they have dartboards and pool tables. Very crowded on summer weekend nights.

eat.name: Susies
eat.desc: A fun subterranean bar with several great microbrews, darts and a great patio during the summer.

eat.name: Hollywood Tavern
eat.desc: Attracts an average looking and refreshingly unpretentious crowd. It's more "meet your friends" than "see and be seen." Albany's largest patio in the summer and a large upstairs for the winter.

eat.name: Common Roots Albany Outpost
eat.desc: Dine with a few beers. The building itself is the old Albany Pump Station, which used to pump the water from the Hudson River up to the reservoir, so the building has a ton of atmosphere and history. A local favorite - no trip to Albany is complete without a visit here.

eat.name: The Hollow Bar + Kitchen
eat.desc: Craft beer and American fare and bands. Another good after-work crowd. Fills with older hepcat college students later in the evening, especially on weekends. Good live music.

eat.name: McGeary's
eat.desc: Often has bands playing Celtic folk and/or bagpipe rock and they have an outdoor area for eating, drinking and listening to live bands during the summer.

eat.name: Waterworks
eat.desc: Another popular gay and lesbian bar.

eat.name: The Fuze Box
eat.desc: A club/event space. Here you find Thursday swing dancing lessons, goth nights, and best known for the weekly Saturday '80s nights. Excellent music, mixed and unpretentious crowds. Dance to Cyndi Lauper with your friends. LGBT friendly!

eat.name: The Washington Tavern (WT's)
eat.desc: An upper classmen bar. It's usually pretty busy.

eat.name: The Pub
eat.desc: A nice place to hang out on weekends. It's very busy with the typical college scene, but slightly more subdued than some of the others.

see.name: Ithaca College
see.desc: Keep an eye out for the free concerts in particular. Worth stopping for the view of Cornell and Cayuga Lake without any events.

see.name: Ithaca Commons
see.desc: is a section of State St. closed to vehicles with shops and restaurants. The Commons has weekly concerts in the summer and hosts numerous Ithaca festivals.

see.name: Cayuga Lake
see.desc: is the largest of the Finger Lakes by surface area. Accessible at Stewart Park, Cass Park, and the Farmer's Market within Ithaca and at Taughannock State Park and Myers Park just outside of Ithaca. Popular activities include Swimming, Kayaking, and Paddleboarding.

see.name: Taughannock Falls State Park
see.desc: Home to the tallest waterfall in New York State. Taughannock Falls is visible at an overlook with no hiking or with 3/4 mile wide and flat trail (1.5 miles round trip). Taughannock Falls is located in [[Trumansburg (New York)

see.name: Buttermilk Falls State Park
see.desc: Swimming, hiking, picnicking, and camping. Even if you can stay for only a minute, you should still come and drive in to see the lovely falls at the lower entrance on Route 13. From the lower entrance you can take a hike up along the falls and gorge; from the upper entrance there is a less strenuous hike around the lake and access to an upper trailhead to the gorge trail.

see.name: Robert H. Treman State Park
see.desc: Swimming, hiking, picnicking, and camping. Hike along the gorge, a relatively vigorous walk if you do the whole loop. Or, you can dip in from the upper entrance and in a short walk see the main falls, Lucifer Falls. The lower entrance area includes one of the more popular swimming spots in the area. It includes a diving board and the ability to swim underneath a waterfall.

see.name: Cascadilla Creek Gorge
see.desc: Easy to get to, free & beautiful. A stone staircase climbs spectacularly along the edge of the falls. The walk up from the entrance at Cascadilla Park up to the exit at College Ave. is an essential part of the Ithaca experience (after all, Ithaca is Gorges!) . Cascadilla Creek Gorge connects downtown and Cornell by trail. Closed from early winter until mid-spring due to icy, dangerous conditions.

see.name: Ithaca Falls
see.desc: Ithaca Falls is {{feet

see.name: Johnson Museum of Art
see.desc: Several of the floors have steady exhibits, but they bring in new art and other, sometimes interactive exhibits several times a year. The 5th floor houses an impressive collection of Asian art but also happens to have one of the nicest views of Ithaca, the Cornell campus, and Cayuga Lake.

see.name: Cayuga Nature Center
see.desc: Cayuga Nature Center has over 5 miles (8 km) of trails and a lodge filled with indoor exhibits including a kids' activity room. TreeTops, their six-story tree house, and 5 miles of trails are open from dawn to dusk. They also offer a wide range of educational activities including environmental, an active outreach program and a "Team Challenge" ropes course.

see.name: Farmers' Market
see.desc: You’ll find wines, and beautiful flowers, unique gifts and specialty foods, clothing and accessories, and an array of paintings, pottery, woodworking, and jewelry offered by fine artists and craftspeople from around the region. Listen to live music or enjoy a waterfront picnic- and don’t forget to sample the burritos, sushi, Sri Lankan cuisine and dozens of other choices from the international cafés.

see.name: Sciencenter
see.desc: The Sciencenter is a hands-on science museum for people of all ages with over 250 fun exhibits, educational programs, an outdoor science park, a seasonal 18-hole miniature golf course, an animal room, and a gift shop. The museum's traveling exhibitions change seasonally and there is always something new to explore. The Sciencenter, named the “2006 Not-for-Profit Organization of the Year” by the Tompkins County Chamber of Commerce, welcomes more than 91,000 visitors per year. The Sciencenter is a proud member of Ithaca's Discovery Trail.

see.name: Cass Park
see.desc: North off Route 89, just outside town. Skating in winter, swimming pool in summer. This is adjacent to Alan Treman State Park, which contains a marina and a large fenced off-leash dog park.

see.name: Kitchen Theatre Company
see.desc: Bold, intimate, engaging. Kitchen Theatre Company is Downtown Ithaca's year round professional theare. Critically acclaimed, this theatre is nationally renowned and offers four performance series (Main Stage, Family Fare, Kitchen Counter Culture, Kitchen Sink). The Kitchen presents an engaging mix of contemporary, regional, and world premiere plays and musicals in an intimate 73-seat theatre that encourages a bold relationship between audience and actor. "Important conversations happen in the Kitchen."

see.name: The Hangar Theatre
see.desc: A professional regional theatre presenting full-scale musicals, beloved classics, comedies, dramas, cabaret, world premieres, and a sparkling lineup of children's plays, musicals and education programs.

see.name: Ithaca College Theatre
see.desc: Performs two musicals, an opera, and several plays each year.

eat.name: Collegetown Bagels/Ithaca Bakery
eat.desc: The Brous & Mehaffey family operates five locations around Ithaca, so [https://www.collegetownbagels.com/ Collegetown Bagels] is something of an Ithaca institution. They offer bagels, sandwiches, and coffee with a whimsical, new-agey feel at reasonable prices. Some of the best authentic bagels and fairly traded coffee, and definitely the most Ithacan. Great for breakfast or lunch.

eat.name: Viva! Taqueria
eat.desc: Maximum calories for your money. Very vegetarian and vegan friendly. Be sure to check out the '''Viva! Cantina''' next door for an expanded menu, table service, and a bar featuring a large tequila selection.

eat.name: Ned's Pizza
eat.desc: Bargain prices on basic and loaded slices. Probably the cheapest fill-up in Ithaca.

eat.name: Lincoln Street Diner
eat.desc: Cheap, good quality breakfasts and lunches. Favored by Fall Creek locals, construction and utility workers. Cash only.

eat.name: Smiley's Mini Mart
eat.desc: Located right off the Ithaca College campus on Route 96B serves the "best pizza on South Hill" by the slice.

eat.name: Shortstop Deli
eat.desc: Specializes in large, delicious subs. Also has breakfast sandwiches, big cookies, soups, and many varieties of coffee. Veg friendly, with veggie burger and seitan subs and vegan chili. Counter service only, but you can sit on the window ledge outside.

eat.name: State Diner
eat.desc: This railroad car diner is one of Ithaca's few 24-hour restaurants.

eat.name: Ling Ling Restaurant
eat.desc: Frequently voted best Chinese food in Ithaca. East Hill Plaza location has large dining room and {{marker

eat.name: Just a Taste
eat.desc: Dinner every day, brunch 11AM-3PM on weekends. Great tapas bar with a large selection of wines available by the glass. You can also select from a number of "flights" of wine, with a small taste of 4 or 5 different wines. The menu changes frequently and usually features local produce. Probably the best "walk in" eatery in town, and has less students than many other places. Tapas range from $4-7. Expect to order 2-4 per person, and expect to share.

eat.name: Maxie's Supper Club and Oyster bar
eat.desc: Maxie's offers dinner daily until 11PM and midnight on Friday and Saturday, and brunch on Sunday until 3PM. Maxie's Supper Club offers a good selection of Cajun seafood food including an oyster bar, as well as authentic southern barbeque. The Cajun fries are delicious, but don't miss the shrimp and grits in tasso sauce, and definitely have lots of the honey butter they serve with the free cornbread. The Supper Club is an excellent place to grab some food and drinks after a late evening event. The restaurant feature locally-produced food and the wine list is award-winningly extensive and also features upstate wines, which often pair well with spicy food.

eat.name: Moosewood Restaurant
eat.desc: Famous world-wide for their vegetarian cookbooks, this downtown institution offers reasonably-priced (for a famous brand) vegetarian fare and fish with a different menu every night and a good selection of local wines, beers and café beverages. Save room for dessert. Ask for a table in the furthest room. In the summer, the street level patio is quite pleasant.

eat.name: Taste of Thai
eat.desc: Taste of Thai has a lovely atmosphere. Heat scale 0-5, where 3 is hot and 5 is "on fire". Try the papaya salad, a curry, or one of the delicious fish or seafood dishes.

eat.name: New Delhi Diamond's
eat.desc: Near the Commons. This restaurant serves a large variety of Indian dishes at dinner, and an $8 buffet at lunchtime.

eat.name: The Heights Restaurant and H Bar
eat.desc: Lunch and dinner. This upscale American-style restaurant is hidden in the ritzy Cayuga Heights area of Ithaca. The menu is definitely among the pricier in Ithaca, but the food is well worth it. This is a great place for a special occasion.

eat.name: Bistro at La Tourelle
eat.desc: Continental French cuisine inspired by a seasoned chef.

eat.name: The Boatyard Grill
eat.desc: Great lively atmosphere right along Cayuga Inlet. Located on a peninsula directly across from Cornell University's boathouse, Boatyard Grill serves greasy food (in good portion sizes). Does not accept reservations but with "call-ahead" you can cut your wait time down significantly. Even with call-ahead, expect to wait awhile on parents' weekends as this is a student's favorite when mom and pop are in paying.

eat.name: Taughannock Farms Inn
eat.desc: see [[Trumansburg_(New York)

eat.name: Level-B
eat.desc: Often with live DJs. Top shelf liquor - although drinks are expensive. It is the only decently clubby place in Ithaca.

eat.name: Loco
eat.desc: Small low key bar with a Mexican theme. Provides nightly specials. More on the pricey side compared to other bars in Ithaca, but is often the least crowded or noisy. Has an upscale, hip atmosphere.

eat.name: Chanticleer
eat.desc: Local hangout on corner of Cayuga and State Street marked by a neon rooster. Downmarket, excellent jukebox.

eat.name: Pete's Cayuga Bar
eat.desc: Popular with both locals and students who enjoy sports and a quiet atmosphere.

eat.name: Simeon's
eat.desc: Restaurant with great food also has a large selection of microbrew and imported beer on tap and bottle, as well as wine.

eat.name: Viva! Taqueria & Cantina
eat.desc: Mexican restaurant that serves Margaritas and has a large selection of Tequila.

eat.name: Uncle Joe's Sports Bar
eat.desc: Roomy sports bar on Green Street separated into a bar area with flat-screen TVs, main dining area for watching sports, and a gaming room with pool table and darts. Also serves American style food.

eat.name: Fall Creek House
eat.desc: Dive bar where you can sit next to Grad students and Vietnam Vets at the same time. Just steps from Ithaca Falls.

eat.name: Northstar House
eat.desc: Restaurant and bar with an outside patio right in the middle of a quiet neighborhood. Often has live music on the patio in the summer.

eat.name: Cayuga Lake Wine Trail
eat.desc: Nestled in the heart of the Finger Lakes is the Cayuga Wine Trail, a 16 winery member organization surrounding Cayuga Lake and offering a unique blend of fine wines.

eat.name: Seneca Lake Wine Trail
eat.desc: Association of 32 wineries surrounding Seneca Lake (next Finger Lake to the west from Cayuga).

see.name: Montauk Point Lighthouse
see.desc: The Montauk Lighthouse is a historical lighthouse with a beautiful view of "The End" of Long Island. It is the easternmost lighthouse on Long Island.

see.name: Hither Hills State Park
see.desc: A beautiful state park that has camp grounds, grills, and beach access and natural areas. It offers families, couples, and individuals a great place to enjoy a day or even a weekend. Great outdoor recreation.

see.name: The Viking Fleet
see.desc: Fishing, whale watching, and other activities.

see.name: Puff ‘N’ Putt
see.desc: A family fun resort with mini-golf, a variety of boat rentals and an arcade.

see.name: Driving Tours
see.desc: Queen City Tours covers most of the center city and surrounding area. They offer different types of tour service for different group sizes. This tour shows Uptown, Dilworth and Myers Park.

see.name: Charlotte 101 Class and Tour
see.desc: Central Piedmont Community College offers a quarterly combination classroom lecture and tour about the Queen City for 6 hours. Pre-registration required.

see.name: Heroes Convention
see.desc: Named "America's favorite comic book convention", Heroes Con has been hosted in Charlotte for the past thirty years and is one of the nations largest and most important comic book conventions. It is held every June in the Charlotte Convention Center and lasts for three days.

see.name: CIAA Basketball Tournament
see.desc: Will come to Charlotte in early March for the next several years. Historically-black colleges from across the country bring their teams, alums and fans to the center city for a week of games. and accompanying parties and conventions. Games are held at Spectrum Center. Other events take place throughout the city, including a festival along Tryon St.

see.name: St. Patrick's Day Parade
see.desc: Is not on the scale of [[Boston]] or [[NYC]], but always well-attended and a fun time to visit the Irish restaurants Uptown. The parade goes up Tryon St., and the best place to view is at the Square.

see.name: Southern Spring Home and Garden Show
see.desc: Has brought designers and experts to the city for nearly 50 years. Held in March at the Merchandise Mart. $9 at the door, kids free.

see.name: PGA Quail Hollow Championship
see.desc: Brings the world's best golfers to Quail Hollow Country Club for a weekend in April. As one would expect, there are plenty of wine-and-cheese events associated with the championship. as well as a noticeable upturn in Polo shirts at Uptown clubs.

see.name: Taste of Charlotte
see.desc: Festival in June is far and away the best time to bring an appetite to the city. Tryon St. closes down for the weekend and many of the city's best restaurants are represented with samples of their signature dishes.

see.name: Scarowinds
see.desc: Is the city's most unique Halloween event. The Carowinds theme park turns ghoulish after dark, with special decor and events. Though it's a bit pricey, it never draws complaints of overpricing. $29, no kids.

see.name: Carolina Renaissance Festival
see.desc: Held in late Fall just outside the city in [[Huntersville]]. It is a family-friendly reenactment of Elizabethan times. Features a wide array of shopping and themed events. $15 for adults, $5 for children.

see.name: Southern Christmas Show
see.desc: In late November is one of the region's biggest holiday shopping events. The Merchandise Mart on E Independence Blvd hosts the event. $8 at the door for adults, $3 for kids. $6 per car to park all day.

see.name: EclecFest
see.desc: Is a fledgling November festival in NoDa, started by the owner of a local bookstore. A combination flea market and cultural festival, this event is a good way to get introduced to the stores and locals of NoDa. Parking is typically available on and around N. Davidson St.

see.name: Charlotte International Auto Show
see.desc: Brings various dealers and buyers together in the Convention Center, usually in November. Adults $8, kids free.

see.name: Carrousel Thanksgiving Day Parade
see.desc: Is one of the city's most beloved annual events. Televised regionally, this parade has run along Tryon St for half a century. A great time to visit.

see.name: Charlotte Collectible and Antique Show
see.desc: Comes to Metrolina Expo on Statesville Rd. each December. The name says it all: shopping opportunities abound. $5, kids free.

see.name: ACC Championship Game
see.desc: The Atlantic Coast Conference, one of the "Power Five" conferences of major college football, holds its championship game at Bank of America Stadium on the second Saturday of December.

see.name: Belk Bowl
see.desc: Another opportunity for college football fans to catch a great game as well as a football-themed festival. Teams from the South's two biggest college football conferences, the ACC and SEC, close out their seasons at Bank of America Stadium. Price varies year-to-year.

see.name: City of Raleigh Museum
see.desc: Local history museum, an excellent place to start your visit to the City of Oaks.

see.name: North Carolina State Capitol
see.desc: Built between 1833 and 1840 and to house the governor's office and cabinet offices. It's now a working capitol and a museum of North Carolina history, especially the period between the building's construction and the Civil War. Several rooms are restored with furniture and items from the era so you can see how they might have looked, including original legislative rooms, a collection of geological specimens, and a library. Full of plaques and informational signs. Gems include spittoons (for tobacco) in the legislative rooms, and a big statue of George Washington in the style of a Roman soldier. Guided tours are available Saturdays at 11AM and 2PM or by appointment for large groups, or take a self-guided tour whenever the building is open.

see.name: N.C. Museum of Art
see.desc: With rotating exhibits, summer outdoor film series, and groovy sculpture garden.

see.name: N.C. Museum of History
see.desc: Extensive museum of North Carolina history, from ancient Native American cultures through colonization and independence up to the World Wars and the Civil Rights Movement. Everything is labeled with thorough and interesting interpretive signs, and some sections have little theater rooms showing videos with more details. Includes a genuine slave cabin rebuilt in the museum, a recreated 1920s drugstore, galleries of North Carolina military history, a children's discovery gallery, and the North Carolina Sports Hall of Fame, which exhibits personal items donated by approximately 360 inductees. Also has a gift shop. Closed for renovation through fall 2028.

see.name: N.C. Museum of Natural Sciences
see.desc: Contains a huge wing full of interactive exhibits, the Nature Research Center, with 3-story multimedia globe structure and exhibits such as a 10,000 gallon (40,000 liter) aquarium.

see.name: Marbles Kids Museum
see.desc: The former Exploris museum has merged with Playspace to form Marbles, an interactive kid's museum, still with an IMAX theater.

see.name: Joel Lane Museum House
see.desc: A Georgian-style manor plantation house built circa 1770 by Colonel Joel Lane, patriot, statesman, and planter, Col. Lane's home has been faithfully restored and is filled with period artifacts. The site houses three historic structures, including a very simple circa 1790 middle-class home interpreted as a kitchen and a circa 1840 Visitors Center.

see.name: JC Raulston Arboretum
see.desc: {{acre

see.name: Governor's Mansion
see.desc: Official residence of the North Carolina governor and family, built in the late 1800s. Group tours are available mid-March to mid-June, but must be booked at least two weeks in advance.

see.name: Mordecai Historic Park
see.desc: Built in 1785, this is the oldest house in Raleigh at its original location. The grounds include the birthplace of President Andrew Johnson.

see.name: Boylan Heights
see.desc: A national historic district from the early 20th century.

see.name: Cameron Park
see.desc: An early 20th-century historic neighborhood, which began as a high-end suburb.

see.name: Five Points
see.desc: A cluster of five suburban neighborhoods set up in the 1910s and 20s.

see.name: Glenwood/Brooklyn
see.desc: "Raleigh's first master-planned neighborhood" was established in the early 20th century as a streetcar suburb for working- and middle-class white families.

see.name: Oakwood
see.desc: The oldest surviving neighborhood in Raleigh, full of historic homes, many carefully restored.

see.name: Mordecai
see.desc: An important historic neighborhood with interesting old houses.

see.name: Raleigh Iron Works
see.desc: Not exactly a historic neighborhood, but a former industrial area that has been redeveloped into a popular industrial-chic complex with a number of restaurants.

see.name: Carolina Hurricanes
see.desc: Raleigh's NHL hockey team plays at [https://www.lenovocenter.com Lenovo Center]. A loud yet friendly atmosphere make this an excellent place to spend an evening during fall and winter. The 'Canes have won the Stanley Cup twice (in 2006 and 2026) and have become famous for their fun "Storm Surge" celebrations after home wins. The Hurricanes have also been one of the NHL's best teams since 2019, and as a result of this success, tickets have risen in price moderately with Lenovo Center filling up close to capacity for most games. Current ticket prices tend to start between $50 and $60 and can be more expensive depending on the opponent and the day of the week. The regular season runs from early October to mid-April, with the playoffs running as late as mid-June.

see.name: Pullen Park
see.desc: Outdoor plays, a 1911 carousel, pedal boats, a miniature train, and an excellent aquatic center.

see.name: William B. Umstead Park
see.desc: Referred to as Umstead park, this state park is accessible by car, bus, or bike, Umstead is a natural haven from the Triangle's urban zones, next to RDU Intl. Airport. Miles of trails, both paved and unpaved, provide access for hikers, campers, bikers and joggers to three lakes and over {{acre

see.name: NC State Wolfpack
see.desc: The sports teams representing North Carolina State University, competing in the Atlantic Coast Conference along with 17 other schools ranging from the East Coast to the San Francisco Bay Area. Football and basketball games are popular in addition to other sports. Most venues are on campus, but the men's basketball team shares Lenovo Center with the Hurricanes.

see.name: North Carolina State Fair
see.desc: Raleigh. One of the largest fairs of its kind in America, this ten-day long event drew almost 940,000 in 2019 to the State Fairgrounds to sample North Carolina produce, attend concerts, ride fair rides and feast on deep-fried Twinkies. Mid to late October.

see.name: Lake Johnson Nature Park
see.desc: A pleasant nature trail winds about 3½ miles (5½ km) around the eastern half of the lake, and another dirt trail exists on the northwestern shore of the lake. Ideal for hiking and biking. Paddle boats can also be rented.

see.name: First Fridays
see.desc: On the first Friday evening of every month, downtown art galleries, museums, and shops stay open late for a downtown-wide event with live music and specials at restaurants and bars.

see.name: Yates Mill County Park
see.desc: A {{acre

see.name: Blue Water Spa
see.desc: Voted best medical spa in America 3 consecutive years. The home spa boutique is a great place to indulge or to pick up a great hostess gift.

eat.name: Big Ed's
eat.desc: Big Ed's signature breakfasts are the Southern standards: homemade biscuits, grits with red-eye gravy, etc. Come Saturday mornings for live Dixieland jazz. Second location on Falls of Neuse Road and Millbrook in Quail Ridge Shopping Center.

eat.name: Farmer's Market Restaurant
eat.desc: Solid, hearty food with fresh ingredients from the state farmer's market right next door. Serves breakfast and lunch.

eat.name: Guasaca
eat.desc: Local chain for Venezuelan arepas. Two locations in Raleigh, vegetarian and vegan options available.

eat.name: Krispy Kreme
eat.desc: The popular Winston-Salem-based doughnut maker is a landmark that nearby residents use to give directions. Look for the "Hot Doughnuts Now" sign for a little round piece of glazed heaven. Quite popular with the students of nearby Broughton and Enloe High Schools, especially in the early morning hours, so plan accordingly.

eat.name: Neomonde
eat.desc: A delicious Mediterranean market and deli. Their fantastic hummus and baba ghanouj with pita bread alone make any meal great.

eat.name: Roast Grill
eat.desc: If you're looking for a hot dog and a bottle of Coke, this is the place in downtown Raleigh. If you're looking for ketchup, though, you may just be asked to leave. Run by a family of Greek immigrants since 1940, in a tiny room added to the front of their house.

eat.name: Watkin's Grill
eat.desc: Greasy-spoon with Civil War memorabilia on the walls. Cash only.

eat.name: Clyde Cooper's BBQ
eat.desc: Traditional NC-style barbecue. A Raleigh institution since 1938.

eat.name: Albaraka Market and Grill
eat.desc: Albaraka Market and Grill in Raleigh is a Mediterranean restaurant with a grocery store. They offer halal food and baked goods.

eat.name: The Fiction Kitchen
eat.desc: Thoughtfully prepared vegan and vegetarian cuisine from a 100% vegetarian kitchen. Very popular among touring music artists playing at the nearby Red Hat Amphitheater.

eat.name: Casa Carbone Ristorante
eat.desc: A family restaurant with an extensive menu that includes everything from classic spaghetti and lasagna, to more intricate entrees such as grouper puttanesca and beef braciole. Excellent wine choices as well. Affordable and delicious.

eat.name: Irregardless Cafe
eat.desc: A Raleigh institution since the 1970s, the Irregardless offers an eclectic menu including creative vegetarian options. Jazz music every night and dancing on Saturday nights.

eat.name: Lilly's Pizza
eat.desc: Part hippie, yuppie, bohemian, and retro, Lilly's is an experience all to its own. It's in the popular Five Points district so parking can be a problem, especially when a popular film is screening at the nearby Rialto theater. If you're adventurous, you can access Five Points by the number 2 CAT bus.

eat.name: Sushi Nine
eat.desc: A great selection of BOGO sushi rolls offered all day everyday. Also offers a mix of Vietnamese, Thai, Japanese, and Chinese entrees. Full bar.

eat.name: The Village Draft House
eat.desc: Don't forget the pickle chips!

eat.name: The Pit
eat.desc: Somewhat upscale whole-hog barbecue. Popular with out-of-staters, but of questionable authenticity.

eat.name: Poole's Downtown Diner
eat.desc: Sourced almost entirely from local farmers and artisan producers, the menu can change on a daily basis. The executive chef, Ashley Christensen, won the 2014 James Beard award for Best Chef in the Southeast.

eat.name: Second Empire Restaurant and Tavern
eat.desc: Gourmet fare in the restored Dodd-Hinsdale House, built in 1879 in the Second Empire Victorian style.

eat.name: The Angus Barn
eat.desc: Fine dining with house-aged steaks.

eat.name: American Meltdown
eat.desc: Gourmet grilled cheese sandwiches and melts on locally baked bread.

eat.name: Baguettaboutit
eat.desc: Locally-produced sausage and freshly-made sauce served inside of a fresh-baked baguette. Vegetarian options available.

eat.name: Belgian Waffle Crafters
eat.desc: Liege (dough-based) and Brussels (batter-based) waffles. Both sweet and savory toppings available. Try the "Choco-waffle", a Liege waffle with chocolate pieces in the dough.

eat.name: Chirba Chirba
eat.desc: Chinese dumplings and dipping sauces. Always a crowd favorite at food truck rodeos.

eat.name: OnlyBurger
eat.desc: Made-to-order burgers and fresh-cut fries.

eat.name: Carolina Brewing Company
eat.desc: In Holly Springs - CBC conducts weekly tours on Saturday afternoons, and it's best to arrive anywhere from 15-30 minutes early to make sure you get a sample of their beer both prior to the tour. No fear if you arrive late, however, as the taps are typically open for an hour afterwards as well. CBC brews an India Pale Ale, a Nut Brown Ale, and the Carolina Pale Ale year round (available at the brewery, in local stores, and in many local bars and restaurants) and usually has one or two seasonal beers available only at the brewery or on tap at select local establishments.

eat.name: Big Boss Brewing company
eat.desc: Big Boss conducts monthly tours on Saturday afternoons, and it's usually best to check the website to find out exactly when. As with CBC, it's a good idea to get there a bit early, as there's usually a pretty good crowd there. Big Boss brews an assortment of seasonal beers that are distributed locally in addition to their year-round Bad Penny Brown Ale, Helles Belle Belgian Blond, and Angry Angel Kolsch Ale that are also sold in bottles at local stores. Big Boss also features an on-site pub called Horniblows Tavern. Though it's not in one of the trendy areas of town, Horniblows is a great place for knocking back a couple of brews and solving the world's problems with your mates.

eat.name: Lonerider Brewing Company
eat.desc: Near the airport and Brier Creek. One of the area's nearest breweries, it has quickly penetrated the market. Often considered a brewers brewery, they offer a handful or more of well-crafted beers. Brewery tours fairly regularly at about once a month.

eat.name: The Raleigh Times Bar
eat.desc: Snug in the offices of the former ''Raleigh Times'' newspaper, this broadsheet turned gastropub is the place for people watching over a pint (or a half pint) of craft-brewed beer.

eat.name: Crank Arm Brewing
eat.desc: Brewpub in the warehouse district that opened in 2013.

eat.name: Fox Liquor Bar
eat.desc: A trendy, upscale bar featuring traditional and creative cocktails along with a small, but interesting selection of craft beers.

eat.name: Raleigh Beer Garden
eat.desc: Popular spot with a huge selection of beer on tap: North Carolina beers on the first floor and beers from around the world on the second floor. Interesting decor too, with a tree growing in the middle of the first floor.

see.name: Battery Park Hotel
see.desc: A 14-story building faced with brick, limestone and terra cotta trim with a Mission Revival style roof, erected in 1924.

see.name: The Biltmore Estate
see.desc: A French Renaissance-inspired chateau; with over 250 rooms, it is the largest single family home in the U.S. and the ''largest privately-owned house in the world'', just a few minutes outside the city and should be on any visitor's itinerary. Basic admission includes access to the fabulous gardens, stables, expansive hiking trails, winery and self-guided house tour.

see.name: Buncombe County Courthouse
see.desc: Completed in 1928, the outside features complex setbacks, window groupings and overlay of Neo-Classical Revival ornamentation. The Neo-Classical interior lobby contains a sweeping marble staircase, bronze and glass screens, a coffered ceiling with ornate plasterwork and a mosaic tile floor.

see.name: Asheville City Hall
see.desc: Designed by Art Deco architect Douglas Ellington and completed in 1927, the City Building is constructed out of Georgia Pink marble, brick, and terra cotta. The steeped, octagonal shaped roof is the logo of the City of Asheville.

see.name: Drhumor Building
see.desc: The Drhumor (pronounced "drummer") is a boldly detailed, Romanesque Revival style building constructed in 1895.

see.name: Grove Arcade
see.desc: Commissioned by Dr. E. W. Grove, the Grove Arcade is an elaborate Tudoresque building occupying an entire city block. It is particularly worth noting, as it was, when it was built in 1927 by architect Charles N. Parker, one of the nation's most unique and interesting buildings. On each side of this city landmark, four giant arches allow entrance into the building. On the main side facing the equally impressive Victorian Battery Park Hotel, are two monumental gryphons, guarding the entrance into the expansive interior, which features oak shopfronts, spiral staircases, and opulence around every corner. Today, it serves as an influential public market with several restaurants, vendors, and mountain craft shops.

see.name: Grove Park Inn
see.desc: Completed in 1913, this historic resort hotel is an important example of the Arts and Crafts style.

see.name: Jackson Building
see.desc: Bordered by South Market Street and South Pack Square, completed in 1925. A Neo-Gothic style skyscraper complete with gargoyles and a bell tower.

see.name: Masonic Temple
see.desc: Features robust brickwork and a tall portico of paired Ionic columns. A three-story, blind arched window is on its Woodfin Street side.

see.name: S & W building
see.desc: Another Art Deco masterpiece designed by architect Douglas Ellington.

see.name: Thomas Wolfe House
see.desc: A sprawling frame Queen Anne-influenced house immortalized in the epic autobiographical novel ''Look Homeward, Angel'' by Thomas Wolfe.

see.name: YMI Building
see.desc: A simplified English Tudor Cottage style with pebble-dashed walls, red brick quoin trim, multi-pane windows and hipped roofs.

see.name: Basilica of St. Lawrence
see.desc: Designed and built in 1905, the Basilica is on the National Register of Historic Places and was elevated in status to a Minor Basilica in 1993 by Pope John Paul II. Features the largest freestanding elliptical dome in North America. This place is gorgeous and a must-see.

see.name: Central United Methodist Church
see.desc: Erected in 1902, the imposing limestone church presents Romanesque Revival style massing and forms, but the detailing more closely reflects the Gothic Revival style. A five-bay loggia, set between two pinnacled towers, fronts the large, gable-roofed auditorium.

see.name: First Baptist Church
see.desc: In Art Deco/Romantic style, Douglas Ellington's first big commission in Asheville. A beautiful distinctive dome with a copper cupola cap.

see.name: First Presbyterian Church
see.desc: Commissioned in 1884, the Gothic Revival style brick nave and tower feature deep-corbelled cornices, hood-molded windows and blind arcading at the eaves.

see.name: Mt. Zion Baptist Church
see.desc: A redbrick late Victorian Gothic church featuring a tin-shingled roof where three towers are topped by ornamental sheet-metal finials. A large number of Art Glass windows ornament the towers and walls. Built in 1919.

see.name: St. Matthias Episcopal Church
see.desc: A Gothic-style building with a gable roof nave. The brick walls are laid with a darker shade of headers presenting a horizontal texture to the building's surface on every face. The interior contains a rich display of well maintained dark woodwork fashioned in various Gothic motifs. The pulpit, lectern, altar and other furnishings are all original to the church and are decorated with trefoil arch panels, quatrefoil incisions and other Gothic elements.

see.name: Trinity Episcopal Church
see.desc: Designed in 1912, the Tudor Gothic Revival style brick building with granite trim features a simple, gable-roofed sanctuary with transepts and a short corner tower.

see.name: American Folk Art & Framing
see.desc: Contemporary Southern folk art, NC wood-fired pottery, and custom picture frames.

see.name: Appalachian Craft Center
see.desc: Authentic mountain handicrafts including pottery, face jugs, quilts, mountain-made toys and handmade rugs.

see.name: Ariel Gallery
see.desc: A contemporary craft cooperative featuring handmade work of local artists. Original works in clay, fiber, furniture, glass, metal, jewelry and book arts.

see.name: Asheville Gallery of Art
see.desc: A partnership of 29 professional, regional artists offering original two-dimensional works from representational to abstract.

see.name: Asheville Glass Center and Gallery
see.desc: A glassblowing school and gallery with daily demonstrations and workshops.

see.name: The Bender Gallery
see.desc: Premier studio glass gallery featuring a variety of glass disciplines by regional and national artists.

see.name: Black Mountain College Museum & Art Center
see.desc: Explores the history and legacy of Black Mountain College.

see.name: Blue Spiral 1
see.desc: Presents contemporary Southeastern fine art and crafts.

see.name: Flood Gallery Fine Art Center
see.desc: Seeks out art that is provocative, challenging, daring, relevant, and important.

see.name: Kress Emporium
see.desc: Featuring more than 100 distinguished artists and craftspeople, all showcased in the historic Kress Building.

see.name: K2 Studio
see.desc: The Kress Emporium's sister gallery.

see.name: Mountain Made
see.desc: Featuring the work of over 80 Western North Carolina artisans.

see.name: Odyssey Gallery
see.desc: Functional and sculptural work by national ceramic artists.

see.name: Studio Chavarria
see.desc: An exclusive members-only salon and fine art gallery.

see.name: Woolworth Walk
see.desc: More than 150 exhibiting artists and artisans selling and making jewelry, fine art, decorative art and crafts in nearly 20,000 square feet of air-conditioned, quality display and studio space.

see.name: YMI Cultural Center
see.desc: Houses numerous exhibits, many dealing with the history of African Americans in Western North Carolina.

see.name: Asheville Art Museum
see.desc: A collection of the very best of 20th and 21st century American art.

see.name: The Smith-McDowell House Museum
see.desc: Asheville’s first mansion and oldest surviving structure.

see.name: WNC Nature Center
see.desc: A living museum exhibiting plants and animals that are native to the Southern Appalachians.

see.name: Asheville Glass Center
see.desc: A glassblowing school, working glass studio, and glass gallery with demos and workshops daily.

see.name: Old Farmers Ball contra dance
see.desc: Asheville is well-known for its scene in contra dance, an easy-to-learn social folk dance with mixed European origins. The main dance takes place at Warren Wilson College, a little outside the city proper.

see.name: Asheville Brews Cruise
see.desc: A personalized tour and VIP treatment at three of Asheville's finest local microbreweries -- Asheville Pizza and Brewing Company, French Broad Brewing Company, and Highland Brewing Company.

see.name: Eating Asheville Tours
see.desc: Eating Asheville’s walking food tour leads you through an orchestration of the finest and most delicious sights and tastes that the city has to offer. Join us for a tour of the city’s unique food culture. Inquire about our walking brewery tours of downtown Asheville!

see.name: Electro Bike Tours
see.desc: Pedal with ease to the Basilica of St. Lawrence, Botanical Gardens, Grove Park Inn, Pack Square, and more on this guided two-hour electric bike tour of Asheville. Also, check out the Bike n Brew Ride!

see.name: Ghost Hunters of Asheville
see.desc: Ghost Hunters of Asheville offer three separate 90-minute ghost tours covering different aspects of historical, haunted Asheville. Guests enjoy free use of ghost-hunting tools and paranormal photographs are guaranteed.

see.name: Herstory Asheville: A Tour that Tells the Rest of the Story
see.desc: Come hear tales of the famous, the infamous, and the unsung heroes of the female persuasion in engaging detail. This 90-minute walking tour covers the history of downtown while spotlighting the women who helped shape Asheville. Tours leave daily from The Old Kentucky Home, Julia Wolfe's former boarding house at Thomas Wolfe Memorial. Reservations required.

see.name: Historic Trolley Tours
see.desc: Sightsee Asheville aboard a vintage Trolley. Fully narrated, covers all major points of interest in Asheville including: the Grove Park Inn, Biltmore Village, the Grove Arcade, the Montford Historic District, the downtown shopping and restaurants district, the Thomas Wolfe Memorial, the Asheville Museum and Art Gallery district, the Asheville Chamber and Visitors Center.

see.name: LaZoom Comedy Tours
see.desc: LaZoom Comedy Tours is "A Tour with a Twist!" You'll get all of the facts plus loads of fun. Your costumed tour guide will take you and your family on a 90 minute adventure covering all of the points of interest. This isn't your grandma's tour (but she can still come).

see.name: Urban Trail
see.desc: A self-guided walking tour in downtown Asheville, tracing the footsteps of Asheville’s historic past. Twenty-seven "stations" are highlighted in this continuous 1.6-mile loop, from churches and buildings to streets and landmarks. Guided tours are available April through November on Saturdays at 3PM. Tours leave from the front desk inside Pack Place. Headsets and maps are available for self-guided tours.

see.name: Montford Holiday Tour of Homes
see.desc: A yearly tour of holiday decorated homes in Asheville's oldest historic neighborhood on the second Saturday of December. Enjoy Shakespearean actors and homemade baked goods during the tour. Located down the street from Asheville Visitors Center.
